name: Idli
description: Household idli made the quicker way with idli rava instead of ground rice, so only the urad dal needs grinding and the batter still ferments to a light spongy steam.

name: Jigarthanda
description: Madurai's layered cold drink: almond gum soaked to a jelly at the bottom, nannari syrup over it, then reduced milk poured down the side so the layers stay visible.
ingredients_json: [{"name": "milk", "unit": "CUP", "notes": "full fat", "optional": false, "quantity": 4, "local_name": "paal", "substitute": ""}, {"name": "sugar", "unit": "TBSP", "notes": "", "optional": false, "quantity": 4, "local_name": "sakkarai", "substitute": ""}, {"name": "nannari syrup", "unit": "TBSP", "notes": "", "optional": false, "quantity": 4, "local_name": "nannari sarbath", "substitute": ""}, {"name": "almond gum", "unit": "TBSP", "notes": "soaked overnight", "optional": false, "quantity": 2, "local_name": "badam pisin", "substitute": ""}, {"name": "vanilla ice cream", "unit": "GRAM", "notes": "", "optional": false, "quantity": 200, "local_name": "ice cream", "substitute": ""}, {"name": "ice", "unit": "CUP", "notes": "crushed", "optional": false, "quantity": 1, "local_name": "pani kattigal", "substitute": ""}]

name: Ela Ada
description: Rice dough spread thin on a wilted banana leaf around a coconut and jaggery filling, then folded and steamed; the leaf is not a wrapper but the source of the aroma.

name: Puran Poli
description: Chana dal and jaggery cooked down to a puran stiff enough to hold a ball, then sealed in a soft wheat and maida dough and rolled thin; the sign of a good one is that the filling shows through without breaking out.

description: Milk reduced by more than half over a low flame, with the skin scraped back in each time it forms, which is what gives basundi its flecks and separates it from a smooth kheer.

name: Mohanthal
description: Besan rubbed with warm ghee and milk and left to sit until it grains up, which is the whole trick; roasted straight from the packet it sets smooth like a barfi and stops being mohanthal.

prep_steps: ["Warm three tablespoons of the ghee with the milk and rub the mixture into the besan with your fingertips until the flour holds together in loose crumbs.", "Leave it to sit twenty minutes; this dhabo is what gives mohanthal its grain, and there is no shortcut for it.", "Pass the rested crumbs through a coarse sieve, breaking up any large lumps.", "Grease a tray and have the nuts slivered before you start, since the last stage moves fast."]
cook_steps: ["Roast the crumbed besan in the remaining ghee on low heat, stirring the whole time, for fifteen to eighteen minutes until it is a deep golden brown and smells nutty.", "In a separate pan boil the sugar and water to a one-string consistency, which is when a drop pulled between finger and thumb forms a single thread, then stir in the saffron milk.", "Take the besan off the heat and pour the hot syrup in, mixing hard and fast; the mixture will loosen and then start to thicken again within a minute or two.", "Stir in the cardamom and nutmeg, pour it into the greased tray and level the top.", "Scatter the nuts, press them in lightly, mark the squares while it is still warm and let it set an hour before cutting through."]

name: Sukhdi
description: Wheat flour roasted in ghee until it darkens, then taken off the flame before the jaggery goes in, since jaggery cooked over heat turns the whole slab hard instead of crumbly.

name: Lapsi
description: Broken wheat roasted in ghee until each grain stands separate, then cooked in three times its volume of water so it swells without going to porridge, with the jaggery stirred in only at the end.

name: Rasgulla
description: Everything depends on the chenna: kneaded until the heel of the hand comes away greasy, and cooked in a syrup thin enough for the balls to swim, because a thick syrup will not let them swell.
ingredients_json: [{"name": "milk", "unit": "CUP", "notes": "full fat, for the chenna", "optional": false, "quantity": 6, "local_name": "dudh", "substitute": ""}, {"name": "lemon juice", "unit": "TBSP", "notes": "diluted with an equal amount of water", "optional": false, "quantity": 3, "local_name": "lebur rosh", "substitute": ""}, {"name": "sugar", "unit": "CUP", "notes": "for the syrup", "optional": false, "quantity": 2, "local_name": "chini", "substitute": ""}, {"name": "water", "unit": "CUP", "notes": "for the syrup", "optional": false, "quantity": 4, "local_name": "jol", "substitute": ""}, {"name": "cardamom powder", "unit": "TSP", "notes": "", "optional": false, "quantity": 0.25, "local_name": "elach guro", "substitute": ""}, {"name": "rose water", "unit": "TSP", "notes": "", "optional": false, "quantity": 1, "local_name": "golap jol", "substitute": ""}]

name: Dhaniya Chutney
description: Ground raw rather than cooked, so the entire job is keeping the coriander green: pulse the mixie in short bursts with chilled water and the leaves stay bright, run it continuously and friction heat turns the chutney a dull olive inside two minutes. Roasted chana dal is what gives it body, letting it sit on a pakora instead of running off the side. The lemon goes in last, after grinding, because acid worked into the leaves early bleaches the colour further. Dairy-free and gluten-free as written, and at roughly 42 kcal a serving it adds a lot of flavour for very little weight, though the raw chilli and lemon make it unkind to anyone with a mouth ulcer.

name: Green Salad
description: The plate salad that comes alongside a North Indian thali, cut into long fingers rather than dice so the pieces stand up on the plate and stay crunchy to the last one. Salting ahead is where it goes wrong: leave the cut vegetables sitting in salt for even ten minutes and osmosis pulls out enough water to leave the tomato slack in a pink puddle, so the salt and lemon belong at the table, not in the kitchen. Chilling the pieces dry, in a covered box, is what keeps them snapping. Undressed it runs about 36 kcal and 2 g of fibre per serving with essentially no fat, which is why it earns its place beside heavy tandoori and rich dal.

name: Kachumber Salad
description: Punjab's chopped salad, where the knife work matters more than the shopping list: onion, tomato and cucumber go into an even fine dice so that no single vegetable takes over a spoonful. The cumin has to be dry-roasted whole in a hot pan until it darkens and smells nutty, then crushed coarsely, because ready-ground cumin powder carries none of the smoke that holds the dish together. Deseed the tomato first, or the salad floods within minutes and the onion goes soft and loses its bite. Sharp with raw onion and lemon, it is what cuts through a rich meat gravy on a Punjabi table, and at roughly 31 kcal a serving it is the lightest thing there.

description: The moong dal is soaked, never cooked: an hour in cold water swells it to a tender bite while keeping the raw, sweet nuttiness that boiling would flatten out entirely. Drain it hard before it goes into the bowl, because dal that stays wet turns the whole salad into a puddle within ten minutes of the lemon going in. Tempered in coconut oil rather than ghee, so it stays fully plant-based as written.

name: Ulli Salad
description: Kerala's raw onion side, and the whole technique is in the cut: slice paper-thin against the grain, because thick slices stay harsh and bully whatever biryani or fish curry they are meant to lift. A ten-minute soak in cold water pulls out the sulphurous bite while leaving the crunch intact, and it is the step almost everyone skips. name: Kakdi Salad
description: Gujarat's grated cucumber salad, sweet-sour rather than chilli-led, with fresh coconut for body and a pinch of sugar that is doing real work in the balance rather than sitting there as an afterthought. Grate the cucumber and wring it out in your fist before anything else goes near it, because skipping that leaves the salt to pull the water out later, and it pools at the bottom and dilutes everything. The mustard and cumin vaghar is poured over while still spitting so the seeds keep their pop instead of going soft. Light and cooling at roughly 57 kcal a serving, though that tempering means it carries a declarable mustard allergen most people would never expect in a bowl of cucumber.

name: Kachumber
description: The Gujarati reading of a chopped salad, and what separates it from its Punjabi cousin is coarsely crushed roasted peanuts and a pinch of sugar rounding off the lemon. Roast the peanuts until the skins loosen and crush them coarse rather than fine, since powdered peanut turns the bowl pasty and buries the fresh vegetable flavour underneath it. They go in at the very last moment, because peanuts left sitting in lemon juice soften and stop being the reason the dish exists. Those peanuts push it to about 3 g protein and 4 g fat a serving, and they make this the one salad in the batch that needs a peanut declaration on the card.

name: Dosakaya Salad
description: Built on dosakaya, the squat yellow Andhra cucumber, which is firmer and markedly more sour than the green kind; swap in an ordinary cucumber and you lose the tang the dish is named for. Peel it and taste a sliver before committing, because a bitter dosakaya cannot be rescued by lemon or salt and it will take the whole bowl with it. Chopped fine with raw onion and green chilli, this is the everyday cooling counterweight on an Andhra plate otherwise built on chilli and tamarind. At roughly 24 kcal a serving it is about the lightest thing that can go on that plate, and it stays raw and plant-based throughout.

name: Mooli Salad
description: Winter radish, cut and then salted and wrung out, a step that looks fussy and is not: radish is very largely water and an unsalted bowl floods in minutes. The trade is that squeezing carries off some of the pepper along with the liquid, so the green chilli and cracked black pepper go in afterwards rather than before. If the bunch arrived with its greens, chop the tender ones in; they are more mineral-dense than the root and most people throw them away. Around 15 kcal and 1.4 g of fibre a serving, though the raffinose in raw radish makes it a dependable trigger for anyone who bloats easily.

name: Dahi
description: Setting curd at home is a temperature problem rather than a recipe: boil the milk to clear out competing bacteria, then bring it down to the point where a clean finger can sit in it for ten seconds without discomfort, which is roughly blood heat. Too hot and the culture dies and you are left with sour milk in the morning; too cool and it never firms past a wobble. Two tablespoons of the previous batch is plenty of starter for a litre, and more culture does not set it faster, it only makes it sour. Left undisturbed somewhere warm for six to eight hours it sets clean at about 105 kcal and 5 g protein a serving; cultured curd is far easier to digest than plain milk, but it is still dairy and out of bounds for lactose intolerance.

name: Onion Kosambari
description: The Karnataka kosambari built on raw onion rather than cucumber, which changes what it is for: sharper, more assertive, and meant to cut a heavy bisi bele bath rather than cool a plain rice meal. The moong dal soaks for an hour and goes in raw, so drain it thoroughly, since dal carrying soaking water thins the whole bowl the moment salt hits it. Onion keeps this version off the festival plate entirely, which is why the cucumber kosambari and not this one shows up as Ram Navami neivedyam. Roughly 6 g of protein a serving from the dal, tempered in oil rather than ghee, so it stays plant-based throughout.

name: Chicken Soup
description: A pepper-led Indian chicken broth, built on bone-in pieces because the collagen in the bones is what gives the liquid body; boneless meat yields a thin, watery result no amount of simmering will fix. Keep it at a bare tremble rather than a boil, since a hard boil emulsifies the fat back into the liquid and the broth turns permanently cloudy. Skim the grey scum off in the first ten minutes and only then add the aromatics, or the pepper and curry leaf get lifted out along with it. About 16 g of protein and 3 g of carbohydrate a serving, which is why it holds up as a light meal on its own rather than only as a starter.

name: Kheera Salad
description: The plainest cucumber salad in the Andhra repertoire and the one that lives or dies on the cumin: dry-roast the seeds until they darken and crush them coarse, because pre-ground powder brings none of the smoke that carries a dish this bare. Cut the cucumber into thick half-moons rather than fine dice, so each piece keeps a snap against the soft rice it is served with. Salt goes on at the table and nowhere earlier, since cucumber is more than ninety per cent water and salting it in the kitchen leaves you with a bowl of brine. At roughly 20 kcal a serving it is the lightest possible counterweight to an Andhra plate of chilli and tamarind, and it stays raw and dairy-free throughout.

name: Ulli Pachadi Salad
description: An Andhra onion pachadi kept chunky instead of ground, so it eats as a salad while still carrying the tamarind-and-chilli backbone of the pachadi it comes from. The tamarind is soaked and squeezed to a thick pulp rather than added as paste, and it has to be thick, because watery pulp turns the onion soggy inside half an hour. The tempering goes over hot and gets stirred in immediately, which cooks the raw edge off the onion just enough without softening it. Sharp, sour and about 45 kcal a serving, and the combination of raw onion and tamarind makes it a poor choice for anyone with reflux.

name: Papad
description: Flame-roasted rather than fried, which is the difference between a two-gram fat side and a deep-fried one: held with tongs a few inches above a live flame and turned constantly, a papad blisters and curls in about twenty seconds. Keep it moving, because the moment it sits still over one spot it scorches into bitterness and the burnt patch cannot be scraped off. Papads absorb humidity from the air and go leathery, so a limp one will never crisp up until it has had a few seconds of dry heat on both sides first. Around 45 kcal each and very high in salt, which is the reason it belongs on the plate as a single piece and not as a snack by the handful.

name: Lasan ni Chutney
description: Kathiawad's raw garlic chutney, pounded rather than blended, because a mixie whips air into it and turns a coarse red paste into a pale pink froth that tastes of nothing. Soak the dry red chillies in just enough warm water to soften them and squeeze them almost dry before pounding, since excess water makes the chutney split and go watery in a day. It is served in tiny quantities beside bajra rotla and sev tameta, and it is meant to be aggressive rather than balanced. Fiercely hot and about 30 kcal a spoonful, and the raw garlic load makes it a genuine problem for anyone with reflux or IBS.

name: Kosumalli
description: The carrot version, and the one people mean when they say kosumalli without naming a vegetable: soaked moong dal, grated carrot, fresh coconut and a mustard tempering, sweeter and softer than the cucumber kind. Grate the carrot on the coarse side of the grater, because fine shreds go limp against the wet dal and the salad loses all its texture within minutes. The dal is soaked and never cooked, so squeeze the sieve dry before it goes in. This is Ram Navami food in Tamil households, served with panakam and neer mor, and it carries about 6 g of protein a serving, which very few salads on a South Indian table manage.

name: Masala Chai
description: The order and the timing are the whole recipe: spices and ginger go into the water and boil hard so their oils come out, tea leaves go in next for barely two minutes, and milk goes in last. Leaves boiled in milk for any length of time release tannins and the cup turns bitter and grey rather than brown, which is the single most common failure. Crush the cardamom and ginger rather than slicing them, because a cracked pod gives up far more than an intact one in the two or three minutes it has. name: Thayir
description: The same set curd as the northern bowl, but set in an unglazed clay pot, which is not decoration: the porous walls wick out a little whey as it sets, so the curd firms up thicker and stays sweeter for longer than it would in steel. Boil the milk, cool it to the point where a finger can sit in it comfortably for ten seconds, then stir in a spoonful of the last batch. In Tamil Nadu and Kerala heat it sets in five or six hours rather than the eight a cooler kitchen needs, and left past that it turns sour fast, which is how it ends up as the next day's mor kuzhambu. Roughly 105 kcal and 5 g of protein a serving, and it is the fixed final course with rice at the end of a meal.

name: Lila Marcha nu Athanu
description: Gujarat's instant green chilli pickle, and everything about it is a moisture problem: a single drop of water in the jar and it grows mould inside a week, so the chillies are wiped dry rather than washed and left wet, and every spoon that goes in must be dry too. The split mustard and fenugreek go in as coarse kuria, not powder, because whole-ish grains soak up the oil and swell rather than turning the pickle into sludge. Oil is heated until it smokes and then cooled right down before it touches the chillies, which kills off spoilage organisms without cooking the chilli soft. Two days in the sun and it is ready; it is fiercely hot, very salty, and about 80 kcal a spoonful, most of that oil.

name: Filter Coffee
description: Everything depends on how the grounds are packed into the upper chamber: pressed down evenly with the plunger disc and hot water poured over in one go, the decoction drips through in fifteen to twenty minutes as a thick dark liquid. Pack it too hard and nothing comes through, too loose and the water races past and you get brown water instead of decoction. The milk must be boiling hot when the decoction meets it, and the mixture is poured back and forth between tumbler and davara from a height, which cools it to drinking temperature and raises the froth. About 92 kcal a cup as made here with a teaspoon of sugar, and the milk means it is not vegan.

name: Dungri Kachumber
description: Onion alone, which is what dungri means and what separates this from the mixed Gujarati kachumber: no cucumber or tomato to soften it, so the dice has to be fine and even or a single spoonful turns into raw onion and nothing else. A pinch of sugar goes in with the lemon, not to sweeten it but to take the metallic edge off raw onion, and leaving it out is noticeable. Salt at the table and not before, because salted onion collapses and floods within about ten minutes. Roughly 34 kcal a serving and entirely plant-based, though a bowl built on raw onion is difficult for anyone with reflux or IBS.

name: Missi Roti
description: Gram flour has no gluten, so a dough made mostly of besan has nothing holding it together and tears the moment it is rolled thin; the wheat flour is structural rather than optional and the ratio cannot be pushed much further. Rest the dough for twenty minutes before rolling, which lets the besan hydrate fully and stops it drinking water out of the surface and cracking at the edges. Roll thicker than a plain roti and cook on a moderate tawa, because besan browns and turns bitter much faster than wheat does. About 12 g of protein a serving, which is the point of it, though the besan and wheat together mean it is not gluten free.

name: Chaas
description: Thin, salted and drinkable rather than the thick sweet lassi it gets confused with: one part curd to three parts water, which is what makes it a digestive at the end of a meal instead of a dessert. Whisk the curd smooth on its own before any water goes near it, because water added to lumpy curd never fully incorporates and the flecks stay suspended in the glass. The cumin is dry-roasted and crushed rather than used as powder, and the curry leaf is bruised and dropped in whole so it perfumes the jug without going bitter. Around 40 kcal a glass, cooling and hydrating, but it is dairy and not an option on a lactose-free diet.

name: Carrot Kosumalli
description: Grate the carrot on the coarse side and not the fine one, because fine shreds go limp against the wet dal within minutes and the whole thing loses the texture it is made for. The moong dal soaks for an hour and goes in raw, sweet and still firm, so drain it until it stops dripping before it meets anything else. Carrot makes this the sweetest of the kosumalli family and the one children will actually eat, scoring well above the cucumber and onion versions on that count. Ram Navami food in Tamil households, tempered in coconut oil rather than ghee, and it carries close to 7 g of protein a serving.

name: Onion Raita
description: Raw onion in curd goes sharp and then bitter as it sits, so this is mixed in the last five minutes before a meal and not held in the fridge for later. Whisk the curd until it is properly smooth first, then fold the onion in, because stirring hard once the onion is already in there breaks the curd and it turns watery. The cumin is dry-roasted and crushed, and the chilli powder is dusted over the top rather than mixed through, so it reads as colour and a little heat on the surface instead of turning the whole bowl pink. About 65 kcal a serving and a straightforward cooling side, though it is dairy and the raw onion makes it hard work for anyone with IBS.

Dice the onion and tomato fine and deseed the tomato, because a wet topping soaks through even faster than a dry one. Roast the papad over a flame rather than frying it, so the base stays brittle enough to snap under the weight of the vegetables. name: Aloo Tikki
description: Boil the potatoes whole in their skins and peel them after, because potatoes boiled peeled and cut take on water and the mash will not hold a shape no matter how much binder goes in. Let them cool completely before mashing, then chill the shaped tikkis for twenty minutes; warm potato falls apart in the pan and cold potato holds its edge. Cornflour rather than breadcrumbs keeps it gluten free and gives a thinner, crisper shell. Shallow-fried on a moderate flame until a deep even crust forms, at about 223 kcal a serving, most of the fat coming from the oil in the pan rather than the tikki itself.

description: The mustard oil has to be taken to smoking point and then cooled right down before it goes anywhere near the garlic, which burns off the raw pungency that would otherwise dominate everything. Pounded dry, with water added a teaspoon at a time only as the mortar needs it, since a wet chutney separates within a day and the garlic goes soapy. This is the one that goes beside dal baati and litti rather than the Kathiawadi version, and the mustard oil is the tell. Fiercely hot at roughly 33 kcal a spoonful, and a raw garlic load like this is a real problem for reflux and IBS.

name: Aam Ka Achar
description: Water is the enemy from start to finish: the mango is wiped rather than washed, the jar is dried in the sun before anything goes in, and every spoon that touches it afterwards has to be dry, or it grows a white bloom of mould within the week. The mango is salted and left overnight first, and the bitter liquid that draws out is thrown away rather than stirred back in, which is the step most people get wrong. Mustard oil goes to smoking point and cools completely before it meets the mango, killing off spoilage organisms without softening the fruit. name: Khajur Imli Chutney
description: Dates and tamarind are simmered together and then pushed through a sieve, and the sieving is not optional: date skins and tamarind fibre both stay stubbornly intact and a chutney full of them feels gritty however long it cooks. Judge the finish by consistency rather than by the clock, taking it off when it coats a spoon and leaves a clear trail across the pan, because it thickens noticeably again as it cools. Dry ginger powder is what stops the whole thing reading as flat sugar, and leaving it out is the commonest reason a homemade batch tastes one-dimensional. Roughly 58 kcal a spoonful, almost entirely sugars from the dates and jaggery.

name: Pudina Raita
description: Mint bruises and blackens the moment it meets a blade, so the leaves are torn by hand or crushed in a mortar rather than chopped, and the difference in colour after ten minutes is obvious. Use only the leaves and none of the stem, which is where the bitterness sits and which no amount of salt will hide. The curd is whisked smooth first and the mint folded in last, so the raita stays pale green with flecks through it rather than turning a uniform grey-green. About 59 kcal a serving, cooling against a biryani, and being curd-based it is out for anyone avoiding lactose.

name: Mixed Achar
description: The winter pickle, made when carrot, cauliflower and turnip are all in season together, and the three have to be cut to a similar size or the cauliflower turns to mush while the turnip is still raw. Blanch them for barely a minute and then dry them in the sun for half a day, which drives off the surface water that would otherwise spoil the jar within a week. Mustard oil is taken to smoking point and cooled completely before it meets the vegetables, and the pickle then needs five to seven days in the sun with a daily shake. About 110 kcal a spoonful, nearly all of it oil, and very high in salt.

name: Cheera Salad
description: Amaranth leaves wilt to almost nothing, so the bunch that looks absurdly large is the right amount, and they need no more than sixty seconds in boiling water before going straight into iced water to hold the colour. Squeeze the blanched leaves properly dry, because cheera holds a startling quantity of water and an unsqueezed bowl sits in a green puddle. Raw coconut oil goes on at the end and is never heated, which is what carries the grassy smell that makes this taste of Kerala rather than of boiled greens. Around 51 kcal a serving with a useful 2 g of fibre, and it is entirely plant-based.

name: Chammanthi Podi
description: Roast the coconut low and slow for twenty minutes rather than fast, because it has to dry out completely before it browns, and coconut that browns while still moist will not keep more than a fortnight. It is ready when the shreds are uniformly deep brown and rattle against the pan like sand. Let everything cool to room temperature before it goes into the mixie, since warm coconut releases its oil under the blade and you end up with a paste instead of a powder. Roughly 40 kcal a spoonful, mostly coconut fat, and being dry it sits in a jar for a month without refrigeration.

name: Boondi Raita
description: Soak the boondi in warm water for ten minutes and squeeze it gently before it goes into the curd, which sounds like it defeats the purpose but is what makes the pearls soft and absorbent rather than leaving them to sit hard and oily in the bowl. Boondi added dry drinks the curd and the raita turns stiff and pasty within a few minutes. Add it last, just before serving, since even soaked boondi eventually breaks down into mush. About 138 kcal a serving, the heaviest of the raitas here because the boondi is deep-fried before you buy it.

description: Chutta means roasted, and the coconut here is taken further than most people are comfortable with: past golden, to a proper dark brown with a few blackened shreds in it, which is where the smoky bitterness that defines the chutney comes from. Stop at golden and it tastes of nothing much. The shallots and chillies go into the same pan and blister rather than soften, and everything is ground coarse on stone or in short pulses, never smooth, so it stays a rough chutney you can see the pieces in. Around 54 kcal a spoonful, mostly coconut fat, and it wants very little water in the grinder.

name: Kaduku Manga Achar
description: Kerala's mustard mango pickle sets itself apart from the northern kind by skipping the sun entirely: the mustard is ground fresh, vinegar does the preserving, and it is ready in two days on a kitchen shelf. Grind the mustard seeds just before use, since pre-ground mustard has lost the volatile compounds that give the pickle its bite. The sesame oil is heated with the fenugreek and curry leaves and then poured over hot, unlike the northern method where the oil must cool first, because here it is cooking the spices rather than sterilising the fruit. About 82 kcal a spoonful and fiercely sharp, and it keeps a year refrigerated as long as the spoon going in is dry.

name: Lemon Sadam
description: Cook the rice a shade firmer than you would for eating plain, then spread it out on a wide plate and let it cool before anything touches it; warm rice tears under a spoon and the whole thing turns to paste. The lemon juice goes in strictly off the heat, because acid held over a flame goes bitter within a minute and there is no rescuing it. Turmeric is stirred into the hot tempering rather than onto the rice, so it colours the oil and coats every grain evenly instead of leaving yellow patches. Around 421 kcal a serving with peanuts and sesame oil doing most of the work, and it travels better than almost anything else on a South Indian table.

name: Milagai Podi
description: Each dal is roasted separately, because urad and chana brown at different rates and roasting them together guarantees one is raw while the other has gone bitter. Take them to an even reddish gold and no further, and roast the chillies last and briefly, since a single scorched chilli makes the whole jar acrid. Everything must come down to room temperature before grinding, or the residual heat steams inside the mixie and the podi cakes instead of staying loose. Grind coarse rather than fine, so it still catches on a spoonful of sesame oil, and it keeps two months dry at about 30 kcal a spoonful.

name: Omelette
description: The South Indian version is closer to a thin savoury pancake than a folded French omelette: the onion and chilli go into the raw egg rather than into the pan first, and the whole thing is cooked through on both sides. Salt the eggs and leave them even a minute and the onion starts weeping water into the mix, which is why it goes in at the last second before the eggs hit the pan. Cook on medium and resist turning it until the top has set to a matte finish, because an omelette flipped while still wet tears down the middle. Roughly 13 g of protein and 5.5 g of carbohydrate a serving, and it is the one egg dish that turns up at breakfast across all five southern states.

name: Idli Podi
description: Each dal is roasted on its own because urad colours in six minutes and chana takes closer to nine, so a shared pan guarantees one is raw and the other bitter. The chillies go in last and come out the moment they puff, since a single blackened chilli turns the whole jar acrid and there is no fixing it afterwards. Everything must fall to room temperature before it meets the mixie, or trapped steam cakes the powder into lumps that never come loose. Ground coarse it clings to a spoon of sesame oil on the idli plate, and at about 31 kcal a spoonful it adds heat rather than weight, though the compounded asafoetida keeps it off a coeliac plate.

name: Pappadam
description: The Kerala one is fried rather than roasted, and it is a different object from the flame-roasted northern papad: smaller, thicker, and it swells to twice its size in a couple of seconds when the oil is right. Test with a corner first, since oil that is not hot enough leaves it flat and greasy, and oil that is too hot browns the outside before the inside has puffed at all. Lift it out the moment expansion stops rather than waiting for colour, because it keeps cooking on the draining rack. Around 121 kcal each counting the oil it actually absorbs, and no Onam sadya is served without one.

name: Perugu
description: The milk is boiled and then brought back down to blood heat before the starter goes in, because culture added to hot milk is killed outright and culture added to cold milk simply sits there. Andhra kitchens set it in a covered steel tumbler left in the warmest corner of the house, where eight hours gives a firm set that cuts cleanly and twelve gives the sourness that pappu and annam actually want. The commonest failure is moving the vessel while it sets, which shears the protein network and leaves a watery layer that never reincorporates. About 98 kcal a serving with 5.3 g of protein, and the fat works out to 51 percent of calories, just under the threshold the corpus uses for a keto tag.

name: Ellu Podi
description: Sesame is the whole dish, so it has to be roasted until it pops steadily and turns one shade darker, and then stopped, because sesame carries a lot of oil and burnt seeds turn the jar bitter in a way nothing masks. Roast it in two batches rather than crowding the pan, since a deep layer steams underneath while the top browns. The urad dal is roasted separately and only briefly, and the mixture is ground in short pulses so the sesame stays granular instead of collapsing into a wet paste under its own oil. About 39 kcal a spoonful and almost all of it fat, eaten stirred into hot rice with a little gingelly oil.

name: Kayi Chutney Pudi
description: Karnataka's version is built on dry copra rather than fresh coconut, which is what lets it keep for a month without refrigeration, and roasted gram gives it the body that would otherwise come from dal. A spoon of jaggery goes in with the tamarind, and the sweet-sour finish is what distinguishes it from the Kerala podi it otherwise resembles. Roast the copra gently and stop while it is still light brown, because dry coconut has almost no water in it and goes from golden to burnt in under a minute. Roughly 37 kcal a spoonful, eaten mixed with a little oil or curd against dosa and rice.

name: Mulaku Chammanthi
description: Nothing is roasted here, which is what separates it from the chutta version: the dry chillies are soaked soft, and everything is ground raw so the heat stays bright and sharp rather than smoky. Squeeze the soaked chillies almost dry before they go into the grinder, since carrying their soaking water in makes a thin chutney that separates by the next morning. Grind coarse on stone if you have one, adding water a teaspoon at a time and no more than two tablespoons in total. Fierce at about 42 kcal a spoonful, and it is eaten in very small quantities with kanji, where a smear against the tongue is the whole point.

name: Curd
description: Set curd is two variables and nothing else: the temperature the milk is at when the starter meets it, and how long it is then left alone. Boil the milk properly first, because unboiled or under-boiled milk carries competing bacteria that give a slack, ropy set with an off smell. A tablespoon of live starter per two cups is plenty; doubling it does not speed the set, it only makes the result sour without ever making it firm. Roughly 98 kcal and 5.3 g protein a serving, entirely from the milk, and it is unsuitable for anyone lactose intolerant however mild the finished curd tastes.

name: Mosaru
description: Karnataka households still set this in an unglazed earthen pot where they can, because the clay wicks moisture out through its wall and gives a thicker, drier set than steel ever does. The trade is that a new pot drinks the first litre almost entirely, so it is soaked overnight before its first use and never scrubbed with soap afterwards. Set it too long in Bengaluru summer and it sours past the point where it will go into mosaru anna; six hours is usually enough in May against nine in December. About 98 kcal and 5.3 g of protein a serving, and the earthen set gives the same macros as the steel one, only a firmer body.

name: Kutchi Machhi Fry
description: Pat the steaks completely dry before the marinade goes anywhere near them, because fish carries surface water and a wet steak steams in the pan instead of frying and then tears when you try to turn it. Thirty minutes of marinating is enough and an hour is too much, since the lemon starts to cure the flesh and it goes chalky. The rice flour coating is dusted on just before frying rather than in advance, and the pan has to be properly hot before the fish goes in and then left alone until the crust releases on its own. About 27 g of protein a serving, with rice flour keeping it gluten free where the semolina version would not.

Grind the roasted masala with coconut to a properly smooth paste, because grit in the paste never disappears into the sambar however long it simmers. Add the ground paste in the last ten minutes only, since coconut boiled hard splits and the sambar turns grainy and dull. About 7 g of protein and 5 g of fibre a serving from the toor dal.

description: Pumpkin collapses if you stir it, so it is cooked covered on low heat and turned perhaps twice with a flat spoon, until the pieces are soft at the edges but still recognisable. The amchur and jaggery go in right at the end together, and the balance between them is the dish; added early, the acid stops the pumpkin softening and you end up with firm cubes in a sweet-sour sauce. Mustard oil taken to smoking point first is what gives it the pungency that makes this a Banarasi puri accompaniment rather than a plain pumpkin curry. It carries no onion or garlic at all, which makes it one of the few main dishes here that is both sattvik and jain-suitable.

name: Majjiga
description: Andhra majjiga is thinner than any other buttermilk in the south, roughly one part curd to four of water, and it is drunk by the tumbler in summer rather than sipped alongside rice. The curd has to be whisked completely smooth before a drop of water goes in, because water added to lumpy curd never disperses and the lumps simply sink. Ginger and green chilli are crushed rather than chopped, which puts their juice into the liquid instead of leaving gritty pieces at the bottom of the glass. At 26 kcal a serving it is the lightest thing on the table, though the salt content makes it a poor idea for anyone watching sodium.

name: Karuveppilai Podi
description: The leaves have to be bone dry before they meet the pan, which means picking them off the stems a day ahead and spreading them out, because a wet leaf steams instead of crisping and the podi will not keep a week. Roast them on the lowest heat until they crumble to dust between two fingers, and stop there; curry leaf goes bitter fast and there is no recovering it. Black pepper rather than more chilli is what gives it the back-of-the-throat heat that distinguishes it from a milagai podi. Roughly 16 kcal a spoonful, the lightest of the podis here, eaten stirred into hot rice with sesame oil.

name: Curry Leaf Podi
description: The leaves have to go into the pan bone dry and come out crisp enough to crumble between two fingers, which takes eight to ten minutes on the lowest flame the burner will hold. Rushed on higher heat they blacken at the edges while the stems stay damp, and that trapped moisture is what turns a jar mouldy in a fortnight. Strip them off the stalk first: the stalk never dries at the same rate and grinds into fibrous threads that catch in the teeth. It comes out dark green-black rather than khaki, about 20 kcal a spoonful, and the compounded asafoetida is the only thing keeping it off a gluten-free plate.

name: Uppinakayi
description: Karnataka's salt-cured lemon pickle, and the cure is the entire method: quartered lemons packed in salt and turmeric and left in the sun for three weeks, during which the skins soften from rigid to yielding and the jar fills with its own juice. Do not add water at any point, and do not open it in the first week, because disturbing the salt crust before it has set is what invites mould. The chilli and mustard go in only after the cure is finished, so the spices stay bright instead of stewing for a month. Around 51 kcal a spoonful, mostly the sesame oil poured over at the end to seal it.

name: Ragi Java
description: Ragi flour clumps the instant it touches hot water, so it is slaked into cold water first and whisked to a completely smooth slurry before any heat is applied, and even then it needs stirring without pause as it thickens. It is ready when the raw grassy smell of the flour has gone and the liquid has turned from dull pink-brown to glossy and translucent, which takes about ten minutes and not less. Drunk warm or cooled with salt in Rayalaseema summers, thin enough to pour rather than spoon. Around 55 kcal a glass with 1.8 g of fibre, gluten free since ragi is a millet, and it is the cheapest calorie on this list.

name: Buttermilk

name: Boomla Fry
description: Bombay duck is close to eighty per cent water and structurally almost nothing, so it has to be salted and pressed under a weight for half an hour before it goes anywhere near a pan, or it disintegrates on contact with the oil. Even pressed, it is handled once and once only: laid down, left alone until the crust sets, turned a single time. The rice flour coating goes on dry and thick, because a thin dusting soaks straight into the flesh and never crisps. About 230 kcal and 20 g of protein a serving, and it is the most fragile thing in this corpus to cook.

name: Kakdi Raita
description: Grate the cucumber and wring it out in a fist before it goes into the curd, which feels wasteful and is not: unsqueezed cucumber releases its water over the next twenty minutes and turns the raita into a thin green soup. A pinch of sugar goes in with the salt, which is the Gujarati signature and what separates this from the North Indian cucumber raita. Fold rather than beat once the cucumber is in, since working it hard splits the curd. Around 65 kcal a serving and properly cooling, though it is dairy and out for lactose intolerance.

name: Chepa Vepudu
description: No flour at all, which is what separates the Andhra fry from the coastal Gujarati one: the marinade itself is thick enough to form the crust, so it is packed on and the fish is left to sit for the best part of an hour. Guntur chilli powder in that quantity is doing colour as much as heat, and it burns easily, so the pan runs at a steady medium rather than high. Curry leaves go into the oil beside the fish rather than on top, where they crisp and perfume the whole thing. About 22 g of protein a serving, and the marinade doubles as the sauce once you scrape the pan.

name: Kondattam Mulaku
description: Green chillies cured in salted curd and then dried in the sun over five or six days, soaked back into the curd each evening and spread out again each morning until they are brittle and pale. The cycle is what forces the curd into the flesh, and cutting it short leaves chillies that stay leathery and go mouldy in the jar. They are stored dry and fried for seconds in hot oil just before a meal, where they puff and turn almost black. The curd makes this a dairy preparation despite what the source list says, and at 24 kcal a piece it is a condiment rather than a side.

name: Kozhi Varuthathu
description: Kerala's dry chicken fry leans on black pepper and fennel rather than chilli, and the marinade wants a full hour because bone-in pieces take that long for salt and acid to reach the bone. Cook it uncovered from the start; a lid traps steam and the chicken poaches in its own liquid instead of frying, which is the single commonest failure. The shallots go in whole and are left to brown properly against the pan, and the curry leaves are added twice, once early and once off the heat. Around 22 g of protein a serving, cooked in coconut oil, and the pan is dry by the time it is done.

name: Kashaya
description: A spice decoction drunk for a cold rather than for pleasure, and the whole method is a long slow reduction: four cups of water down to two over fifteen minutes, so the pepper and dry ginger actually leach out instead of just floating. Crush the whole spices coarsely first, because intact peppercorns and cardamom give up almost nothing in a quarter of an hour. The jaggery goes in off the heat, since boiling it in scorches the sugars and turns the decoction bitter behind the sweetness. Tulsi is added last of all and steeped rather than boiled, and about 48 kcal a cup, all of it the jaggery.

name: Chicken Nu Shorba
description: Tomato-led where the Kerala broth is pepper-led, and thickened by the tomatoes breaking down completely rather than by any flour, so they need a good ten minutes on their own before the water goes in. The whole garam spices are bloomed in oil at the start and left in the pot rather than ground, which gives a clean aromatic broth instead of a muddy one. Keep it at a simmer once the chicken is in, because a hard boil clouds the liquid and toughens the meat at the same time. Roughly 16 g of protein a serving, and the lemon goes in off the heat at the very end.

name: Neer Majjige
description: Far thinner than the Gujarati chaas, roughly one part curd to five of water, which is the point rather than an economy: it is drunk by the glass in Karnataka summers and at temple counters, not sipped as a digestive at the end of a meal. The ginger and green chilli are crushed rather than chopped so they release into the water without leaving pieces to strain out. Nothing is tempered and nothing is heated, so the curry leaf has to be bruised hard between the palms to give anything at all. Barely 27 kcal a glass, cooling and genuinely hydrating, but it is dairy and stays out of reach on a lactose-free diet.

name: Matar Pulao
description: Soak the basmati for thirty minutes and then drain it properly, because grains that go into the pan wet break at the tips and the pulao turns sticky instead of separate. The water ratio is one and two-thirds to one by volume and not the two-to-one used for plain rice, since soaked grains have already taken up their share. Once the lid goes on, leave it entirely alone for the full fifteen minutes and then another ten off the heat; lifting it to check releases the steam that finishes the cooking. Around 398 kcal a serving, cooked in oil rather than ghee so it stays plant-based.

name: Putani Chutney
description: Roasted gram is already cooked, so nothing here needs a pan except the tempering, and the chutney comes together in the mixie in under two minutes. It thickens noticeably as it stands, because the gram keeps drinking water for the first ten minutes, so grind it looser than you want it and check again before serving. Tamarind rather than lemon is what carries the sourness in the Karnataka version, and it goes into the grinder rather than being stirred in after. About 100 kcal a serving, thick enough to hold on a dosa without sliding off it.

name: Neer Mor
description: What separates neer mor from plain buttermilk is the asafoetida, which goes in as a pinch dissolved in a spoon of water rather than sprinkled dry, or it clumps and sits on the surface in brown specks. Tamil kitchens keep it deliberately thin and very lightly soured, which means yesterday's curd rather than today's, and it is served in the afternoon rather than with the meal. Crushed ginger and curry leaf are steeped and then strained out, so the glass carries their flavour with nothing in it to chew. Around 27 kcal a glass, and the compounded asafoetida is the reason this row does not carry a gluten-free tag.

name: Paruppu Podi
description: Milder than a milagai podi and built on dal rather than chilli, which is why it is the podi given to children and to anyone recovering from illness, mixed into hot rice with a spoon of ghee. The toor and chana dal are roasted separately to the same pale gold, since toor colours faster and roasting them together leaves one of the two raw. Black pepper does the heat instead of a fistful of chillies, and only six go in. Around 23 kcal a spoonful, and ground slightly coarse so it takes up ghee rather than clumping into it.

name: Sukku Coffee
description: There is no coffee in it, which catches people out; the name comes from the colour and from being drunk in place of one. Dry ginger is the whole backbone, so it goes in crushed rather than as powder, and the coriander seeds are dry-roasted first, which is the step that gives it the roasted depth the name promises. Palm jaggery rather than cane changes it more than it sounds, bringing a smoky edge that ordinary jaggery does not. Around 62 kcal a cup and drunk hot in Tamil Nadu through the rainy months, particularly for a cough.

name: Magaya
description: What sets the Andhra pickle apart is that the mango is dried before it is spiced, not after: the cubes are salted, then spread in the sun for three days until they are leathery and have lost most of their water. Only then do they meet the mustard and chilli, and the oil poured over rehydrates them slowly into something chewy rather than soft. Grind the mustard fresh and coarse on the day, because pre-ground mustard has lost the volatile heat that this pickle is named around. Roughly 94 kcal a spoonful, nearly all of it sesame oil, and it keeps a year if the spoon stays dry.

name: Happala
description: Karnataka happala is held with tongs an inch above a live flame and turned constantly, which blisters it white in about twenty seconds a side without any oil at all. Left still for even three seconds it scorches in one spot and the burnt patch tastes bitter across the whole disc. Take it off while it still has a faint give, because it crisps further as it cools and a papad roasted to crisp on the flame will be brittle and dusty by the time it reaches the plate. At 45 kcal a piece it is the cheapest crunch on a meal, and dry-roasting keeps it there against the 120 kcal a deep-fried one costs.

name: Beans Thoran
description: The cut is the dish: beans chopped as fine as the coconut is grated, so a spoonful reads as one thing rather than as beans with coconut scattered over them, and that is twenty minutes of knife work there is no way around. The coconut is crushed with the green chilli, shallot and cumin rather than added loose, which is what makes a thoran instead of a stir-fry. Three tablespoons of water and a lid for eight minutes is all the moisture it gets, and then the lid comes off so the last of it steams away. About 172 kcal a serving and almost 5 g of fibre, cooked entirely in coconut oil.

description: Fenugreek rather than mustard is the lead here, four tablespoons of split methi kuria against two of rai, and that bitterness is the point rather than a flaw to be balanced out. Groundnut oil instead of mustard oil is the other Gujarati marker, and it goes in cold after being heated and cooled, so it seals rather than cooks. The mango is salted overnight and drained but never sun-dried, which leaves the cubes firmer and crunchier than in the Andhra version. Roughly 93 kcal a spoonful and it needs three days before the kuria has softened enough to eat.

name: Vadiyalu
description: Ground urad dal batter piped into small drops on a cloth and dried in the sun for four days, then stored and fried a handful at a time before a meal. The batter has to be beaten until a spoonful floats in water, because unaerated batter dries into hard pellets that never puff in the oil. Pipe them onto cloth rather than a plate, since anything they can stick to will tear them when they come off. Fried, they take about six seconds and swell to twice their size, at roughly 37 kcal each, and the dried ones keep the better part of a year in a jar.

description: The quick Andhra lemon pickle, which skips curing altogether: the lemons are steamed briefly to soften the skins, then mixed with the spices and eaten within two days. Roughly 58 kcal a spoonful, almost all of it the sesame oil that goes over the top.

name: Shikanji
description: What separates it from plain lemonade is the black salt and the roasted cumin, and both need to be dissolved in a little water first, because dropped straight into a full jug they sink and the last glass tastes of nothing but salt. Roast the cumin whole and crush it rather than using powder, which is flat by comparison. The mint is bruised in the palm and dropped in whole rather than muddled, so it perfumes the jug without turning it green and bitter. Around 52 kcal a glass with four tablespoons of sugar across four, and it is the cheapest thing to make in this corpus.

Sesame oil in quantity is doing the preserving, at roughly 61 kcal a spoonful, and there is no sun-drying involved at any point.

name: Nimbekayi Uppinakayi
description: The lemons are quartered but left joined at the base so they hold their shape through three weeks in brine, and they must be wiped bone dry before cutting because a single drop of water on the knife is enough to start mould in the jar. Salt alone does the first three weeks of work, softening the rind until a fingernail goes through it without resistance; only then does the chilli and tempered oil go in, since chilli added at the start bleeds colour and turns muddy brown by the time the pickle is ready. description: Thick where the chaas is thin, and the ratio is the difference: two parts curd to one of water rather than one to three, so it is spooned as much as drunk. name: Uble Ande
description: Start the eggs in cold water rather than dropping them into boiling, which is the difference between shells that peel cleanly and shells that take half the white with them. Eleven minutes from the moment the water boils gives a firm yolk with no grey ring; twelve gives the ring and a chalky texture. Straight into iced water afterwards, which stops the cooking and contracts the egg away from the shell. Dressed with black salt, roasted cumin and lemon it becomes a street snack rather than a plain boiled egg, at about 13 g of protein a serving.

name: Nimbu Ka Achar
description: No oil at any point, which makes it the only fat-free preserve in this corpus: the lemons cure in nothing but their own juice and a great deal of salt over three weeks in the sun. The jar has to be shaken daily so the salt redistributes and every quarter stays submerged, and any piece left proud of the liquid will grow mould. name: Mavinakayi Uppinakayi
description: Karnataka cures its mango in brine rather than in dry salt or oil, which is the whole distinction: the cubes sit submerged in salted water for a fortnight and come out firm and translucent rather than shrunken. The brine has to be strong enough to float a raw mango cube, and a weak brine ferments instead of curing. Byadgi chilli goes in at the end for colour more than heat, and the oil is a thin seal on top rather than a medium. Roughly 41 kcal a spoonful, and the cured cubes keep their snap in a way the dry-salted pickles do not.

name: Murgh Shorba
description: A shorba is judged on clarity, and clarity comes from never letting the pot reach a rolling boil once the chicken is in; a bare shiver at the surface for forty minutes extracts the collagen without churning the fat back into the liquid. Skim the grey scum in the first ten minutes and keep skimming, because anything left floating at that stage is what makes the finished broth cloudy and faintly sour. Bone-in pieces are not optional here, since the body of the soup comes from marrow and cartilage rather than the meat. Around 192 kcal and 26 g of protein a bowl, which makes it one of the few genuinely high-protein rows that is still low carb.

name: Kobbari Pachadi
description: Coconut-led rather than gram-led, which is what separates the Andhra chutney from the Karnataka putani one, and the roasted gram here is only a thickener rather than the substance. Garlic goes in raw with the coconut, two cloves and no more, and it is the thing people notice without being able to name. Grind it thick enough to hold a ridge, because a thin coconut chutney separates into water and solids within the hour. About 97 kcal a serving, most of it coconut fat, and it wants eating the day it is made.

name: Nimbu Achar
description: This is the oil-free Punjabi version, where the lemons cure in nothing but their own juice and salt, so the jar has to be filled to the brim and shaken daily to keep every piece submerged. Any wedge that sits proud of the liquid grows a white bloom within a week and the whole batch has to be thrown. Black salt and ajwain go in only after the rind has softened, around week four, because both lose their aroma if they sit through the full cure. It darkens from yellow to near-black over six weeks, which is the sign it is ready, not a fault, and at 9 kcal a wedge it is the lightest condiment in the corpus.

name: Beans Vepudu
description: No coconut anywhere, which is the line between an Andhra vepudu and a Kerala thoran, and without it the dish depends entirely on getting real colour on the beans. That means an uncovered pan and enough patience to leave them alone in between stirs, because a lid steams them soft and green and the whole point is the browned, slightly shrivelled edges. The garlic goes in whole and crushed rather than minced so it survives twenty minutes without burning. Around 155 kcal a serving, fried in groundnut oil, and the beans should still resist a little when they come off.

name: Chaas Vaghareli
description: The tempering is the entire difference from plain chaas, and it goes in hot, straight from the pan into the cold buttermilk, where it hisses and seizes. Pour it in a thin stream while whisking, because dumped in at once the hot oil shocks the curd and it curdles into visible flecks. Asafoetida goes into the oil at the very end and off the heat, since it burns in about two seconds and turns the whole jug acrid. Around 71 kcal a glass, and unlike the plain version this one is drunk at room temperature rather than chilled, so the tempering stays aromatic.

name: Kheera Raita
description: Grate the cucumber and then squeeze it, because a cucumber is ninety-five percent water and any of it left behind turns the raita into a thin green soup within twenty minutes of sitting on the table. Save the squeezed liquid and use it to loosen the curd instead of plain water, which keeps the flavour and the body. The curd should be whisked before the cucumber goes in, never after, since stirring shredded cucumber into thick curd breaks the strands and releases more water again. At 66 kcal a bowl it is the lightest way to cool a hot plate, and the raw cucumber makes it one of the few raitas that genuinely should not be made ahead.

name: Aloo Tamatar Sabzi
description: No onion and no garlic at all, which is deliberate rather than a restriction: the asafoetida in the hot oil does the savoury work they would otherwise do, and it is the reason this turns up on fasting days and in temple kitchens. Break the boiled potatoes by hand into rough pieces rather than cubing them, since the torn surfaces catch the gravy where clean cut faces shed it. The tomatoes need to cook right down until the oil separates, and rushing that leaves a thin sauce that tastes raw. About 180 kcal a serving, and it thickens further as it stands, so keep it looser than you want it.

name: Cabbage Vepudu
description: Cabbage is mostly water and it will steam itself if the pan is crowded, so it goes into a wide kadai on high heat and gets spread out rather than piled up. Shred it thin and dry it properly after washing, because water clinging to the leaves is the difference between a fry and a stew. Salt goes in only in the last five minutes, since salted early it draws out the moisture you have spent fifteen minutes driving off. About 115 kcal a serving, browned at the edges and still with a little crunch left in the ribs.

name: Kerala Matta Rice
description: Parboiled red rice behaves nothing like white rice: it wants soaking, a great deal more water and around forty-five minutes, and it is cooked in excess water that gets drained off rather than absorbed. The grain stays firm at the centre long after white rice would be mush, so judge it by pressing a grain flat rather than by the clock. The starchy water poured off is kanjivellam and is drunk rather than thrown away. About 250 kcal a serving with more than twice the fibre of polished rice, and the bran is why it takes so long.

name: Khichiya Papad
description: Rice flour rather than urad dal, which changes what it does in the heat: it blisters into large translucent bubbles instead of curling flat, and it needs a good deal more time over the flame than a dal papad. Roast it further than feels right, until the bubbles have gone from white to pale gold, because pulled off early it stays chewy in the middle rather than shattering. Being rice-based it carries no asafoetida and so is genuinely gluten free, unlike the urad dal papad in this corpus. Around 65 kcal each, and it goes soft within minutes in humid weather.

description: A rasam built on chicken rather than a chicken soup: thin, sharply sour with tamarind, and drunk from the bowl or poured over rice rather than eaten with a spoon. The chicken goes in bone-in and is simmered long enough to give up its collagen, but the tamarind is added only in the last ten minutes, because acid early on stops the meat softening and it stays stringy. Crushed pepper goes in twice, half during the simmer and half off the heat, which keeps the sharpness rather than letting it all cook flat. Roughly 11 g of protein a serving at 145 kcal, and it is thinner than any gravy in this corpus.

name: Idli Karam Podi
description: The garlic is what separates the Andhra karam podi from every other idli powder, and it has to be roasted whole with the skin on until the cloves are papery and brittle, roughly twelve minutes on low heat. Roasted peeled, garlic sticks and burns; roasted damp, it grinds into a paste that makes the whole batch clump and go rancid inside a fortnight. Guntur chillies are used in a quantity that looks alarming, but the dal absorbs most of the heat and the point is a podi that stands up to being eaten with plain idli and oil. It comes out around 29 kcal a spoonful, and the compounded asafoetida is what keeps it off a gluten-free plate.

name: Safed Makhan
description: Churned from set curd rather than from cream, which is why it comes out white instead of yellow and tastes faintly sour. Temperature decides everything: the curd must be properly cold and the water iced, because at room temperature the fat stays dispersed and you can churn for twenty minutes without a grain of butter appearing. It gathers suddenly rather than gradually, so once flecks start forming stop and collect rather than carrying on. A litre of curd yields only about forty grams, which is why it is a treat, and what is left in the pot is chaas.

name: Avalakki Bath
description: The rinse decides the dish. Thick poha goes into a colander and is run under the tap for about fifteen seconds, then left to sit for ten minutes and finish softening on its own moisture, and any longer under the water gives a pan of paste. Test a flake between two fingers before it goes anywhere near heat: it should crush without resistance but still hold its shape. Peanuts are fried first and separately so they stay crisp against the soft poha, and the lemon goes in off the heat. Around 300 kcal a serving, and it is the fastest full breakfast in this corpus.

name: Nuvvula Podi
description: Sesame is almost half fat, so it roasts in about ninety seconds and goes from nutty to bitter in the next thirty; pull the pan off the moment the seeds start jumping and popping rather than waiting for colour. Grind it cold and in short bursts, because any warmth at all presses the oil out and what should be a loose powder turns into a dense paste that will not keep. The dal here is a thickener rather than a flavour, which is why so little of it goes in relative to an idli podi. It is the most calorie-dense podi in the corpus at about 43 kcal a spoonful, and at 65 percent of calories from fat it is the rare condiment that clears the house keto threshold.

name: Narthangai Oorugai
description: Citron is not lemon: the peel is thick, pithy and genuinely bitter, and that bitterness is what the pickle is for rather than a defect to be salted out. The pieces are salted and dried in the sun for a week until they shrink and darken to a deep brown, which concentrates rather than removes it. Eaten in very small quantities with curd rice, traditionally at the start of a meal because the bitterness is held to sharpen the appetite. Around 45 kcal a spoonful, and a whole citron makes enough to last a household most of a year.

name: Vathal
description: Turkey berries cured in salted curd and dried over five days, soaked back into the curd each evening and spread out again each morning until they rattle. The bitterness is the reason for the dish rather than something to be cured out, and the curd tempers it without removing it. Crush each berry lightly before it goes into the curd so the cure reaches the inside, or the centres stay green and go mouldy in the jar. Fried for a few seconds before a meal, they turn near-black and crackle; the curd in the cure makes this a dairy preparation despite what the source list says.

name: Sukku Malli Coffee
description: The coriander seed is what the malli in the name refers to, and it must be dry-roasted and coarsely crushed rather than used whole, or it floats and gives up almost nothing in fifteen minutes of simmering. Dry ginger goes in as a broken piece rather than powder, because powder clouds the decoction and leaves a gritty layer at the bottom of the tumbler. Add the palm jaggery only after the pot comes off the heat, since boiling jaggery turns the drink faintly bitter and darkens it past the amber it should be. About 61 kcal a tumbler and almost all of it is the jaggery, which puts it just inside the low-carb line at 14.1 g.

name: Sandige
description: The rice has to be ground to a batter and then cooked into a thick, glossy paste before it is piped, because raw batter spreads into a puddle on the sheet and dries into a wafer that shatters instead of puffing. The paste is worked while still hot, which is unpleasant but necessary; cooled, it stiffens and will not pass through the piping cloth at all. Three full days of hard sun are the minimum and there is no shortcut, since a sandige that is dry on the surface and damp inside will spit violently in the oil and then go leathery. Counting only the 40 ml or so actually absorbed rather than the panful it fries in, each works out at about 56 kcal.

name: Millet Pongal
description: Little millet swells more than rice and sets far harder as it cools, so it takes five parts water to one of grain rather than the four you would use for rice pongal, and it still wants loosening with hot water at the table. Roast the moong dal until it smells nutty before the millet goes in, which is what stops the whole thing tasting flat. Crush the peppercorns coarsely rather than using powder, because whole pepper found in a mouthful is part of what pongal is. Around 359 kcal a serving, cooked in coconut oil rather than ghee so it stays plant-based.

name: Seeraga Samba Rice
description: A small, dense, cumin-shaped grain that behaves nothing like basmati: it takes less water, cooks faster and goes from done to mush inside two minutes, so it is watched rather than timed. Soak it twenty minutes and use one and two-thirds parts water, not the two you would give a long grain. It absorbs far more flavour than basmati, which is why Chettinad biryani is built on it, but plain it is simply a firmer, nuttier rice. Around 270 kcal a serving, and it costs noticeably more than everyday rice.

name: Karikku
description: The least prepared thing in this corpus and still a skill: a tender coconut is opened by shaving the top down at an angle with a heavy knife until a small window appears over the water, and cut too deep the whole thing spills. Pick one that sounds full and heavy rather than hollow when tapped. The water is drunk first and then the shell is split so the soft translucent malai can be scraped out with a piece of the husk, which is the proper spoon for it. About 58 kcal a serving with the malai counted, and it is the most hydrating thing on the list.

Turmeric goes in with the onion rather than at the end, so it colours the oil and every piece takes it evenly. About 186 kcal a serving, finished with lemon and coconut off the heat.

name: Rasam
description: It must never boil. Once the tamarind broth has taken the dal water it is brought only to the point where a white froth rises at the edges, and boiling past that turns it cloudy and flattens the pepper entirely. The rasam powder is ground fresh from pepper, cumin, coriander seed and red chilli, and a shop-bought powder is the single thing that most changes how this tastes. Garlic is crushed with its skin on and thrown in whole. Around 75 kcal a serving, thin enough to drink, and it is poured over rice as much as it is spooned.

name: Nannari Sarbath
description: Sarsaparilla root syrup, lemon and soaked basil seeds, and the seeds are the part people get wrong: they need twenty minutes in water to swell into their translucent jelly coats, and dropped in dry they sink and stay hard. Add the syrup to the water before the lemon, because lemon poured onto concentrated syrup makes it seize into strands. It is drunk through Tamil summers for its cooling reputation as much as its taste. Around 92 kcal a glass, almost entirely the syrup, which is bought rather than made here.

name: Tori Sabzi
description: Ridge gourd is more than ninety per cent water and it all comes out in the pan, so this is cooked uncovered from the moment the gourd goes in and no water is ever added. Peel the ridges off but leave the pale green skin between them, which is what holds the pieces together as they soften. It collapses from firm cubes to a soft mass in about fifteen minutes and that is the intended finish rather than overcooking. Around 110 kcal a serving, and asafoetida does the savoury work in place of the onion in the strictly vegetarian version.

name: Karivepaku Podi
description: The Andhra version puts roasted garlic into what is otherwise a curry leaf powder, which shortens its life to about a month but gives it the pungency that plain rice needs. Leaves and garlic cannot share a pan: the leaves are done in eight minutes and the garlic needs twelve, and a shared roast leaves one scorched and the other damp. Tamarind goes in as a dry pinch rather than pulp, because any moisture at all in a podi is what turns a jar mouldy in the third week. At about 18 kcal a spoonful it is among the lighter podis, and the compounded asafoetida is the only reason it is not gluten free.

name: Kobi Vatana nu Shaak
description: Cabbage and peas with a mustard and cumin vaghar, no onion or garlic at all, and a teaspoon of sugar with the lemon at the end that is the Gujarati signature rather than an afterthought. The cabbage goes in on high heat and spread wide, because piled up it steams and the shaak turns watery instead of staying separate. Peas go in only for the last five minutes, since cooked from the start they wrinkle and lose their colour. About 136 kcal a serving, and it is one of the few main-course rows here that is sattvik as written.

name: Keema Pav
description: The mince goes into the pan in a thin layer and is left alone until it browns, because stirred early it gives up its water and simmers itself grey and grainy instead of catching on the base. Garam masala is folded in off the heat rather than fried with the powdered spices, since four minutes in hot oil cooks the cardamom and mace straight out of it. The pav are pressed cut-side down in butter on a hot tawa for about a minute a side, long enough to crisp and no longer, or the crumb dries out and stops soaking anything up. Two pav a head puts the plate at 67 g of carbohydrate and 672 kcal, the heaviest serving authored so far, and almost all of that carbohydrate is the bread rather than the keema.

name: Ulli Karam
description: The onion goes into the mixie raw alongside the roasted chillies rather than being fried first, which is what keeps the karam sharp and faintly sweet instead of tasting like a cooked chutney. Pulse it, do not run the grinder: held down continuously the onion gives up its water, the paste slackens to a pink slurry and it will not keep the week it should. Tamarind is doing as much preservation work here as it is flavour. Twelve chillies across twelve servings comes to about 41 kcal a spoon carrying all of the heat, so it is smeared thin on dosa rather than served as a side.

name: Bhinda nu Shaak
description: Okra is fried in a wide uncovered pan and left completely alone for the first six minutes, because the slime only sets while the cut faces are still wet and stirring early is exactly what turns the shaak ropey. Wipe the pods dry before they are cut and keep the knife dry too; water on the blade is the other route slime takes in. Amchur and a teaspoon of sugar go in at the very end, the sweet-sour finish that a Punjabi bhindi would never carry. It contains asafoetida, so despite the source list marking it gluten free this row does not get the tag.

name: Kerala Idli
description: Rice and dal are ground separately and to deliberately different textures, the dal to a smooth aerated cream and the rice to a fine grit you can still feel between your fingers, and grinding them the other way round gives dense idlis whatever the fermentation later does. The poha is the Kerala touch and it is structural rather than decorative, holding water so the idli stays soft for hours instead of tightening as it cools. Batter should rise by about half, not double; over-fermented batter smells sour and sinks in the steamer. Below roughly 25 degrees the ten hours quoted here will not be enough, which is the single reason this recipe fails in an air-conditioned flat.

name: Southekayi Palya
description: The cucumber is halved lengthways and the seed core scraped out before it is cubed, because the pith cooks to slime and drags the rest of the palya down with it. It is covered for barely eight minutes and checked early, since the flesh crosses from firm to collapsing in about ninety seconds and there is no way back. The teaspoon of jaggery is not there to sweeten so much as to balance the raw bitterness that shows up near the stem end of an older gourd. Fat runs to 66 per cent of calories on the coconut oil and grated coconut, which is why this modest-looking vegetable row qualifies as keto where several richer ones in the corpus do not.

name: Kandi Podi
description: Toor dal is the bulk here and it is the hardest of the dals to roast evenly, needing a full ten minutes on low heat with constant movement before it turns an even biscuit brown. Pulled early it tastes raw and chalky in the mouth; pushed to dark brown it turns the whole podi bitter, and unlike a chilli you cannot pick the offending grains out. The powder must be ground coarse enough to still feel gritty, because a fine grind packs down in the jar and stops taking up ghee on the plate. About 32 kcal a spoonful, mostly carbohydrate from the dal, which is why a keto claim would not hold up here.

name: Ragi Sangati Natukodi
description: Country chicken is not broiler chicken and will not come tender in twenty minutes, so it goes into the pressure cooker for four whistles before the masala ever touches it; skip that and the meat fights back at the table. The sangati is beaten rather than stirred, ragi flour rained into boiling rice and worked hard against the side of the pot until no dry pockets are left, because a seam of raw ragi through the middle is the standard failure and is only discovered once it is on the plate. Ball it while it is still too hot to hold comfortably, since it stiffens as it cools and will not shape at all when cold. The ragi rather than the rice is why this is field food: it carries over half of the 7 g of fibre a serving on its own, against barely a tenth of a gram from the rice.

description: The beans are cut short and cooked covered for the first eight minutes so they steam in their own moisture, then uncovered to dry off, which is what keeps them bright rather than the olive colour of beans boiled in water. Crushed roasted peanuts go in at the very end and are the difference between this and any other bean side; stirred in early they soften and the whole point is lost. Sugar and lemon arrive together off the heat in the Gujarati way. It contains asafoetida, so the source list's gluten free flag does not survive, and at 12.5 g of carbohydrate the keto flag does not either.

name: Pavakka Kondattam
description: Bitter gourd is sliced thin, salted hard and left to weep before it ever meets the curd, because the water it gives up carries out a good part of the bitterness and skipping that step makes a kondattam nobody finishes. The curd cure is not a marinade, it is the drying medium: the slices are soaked, spread out, dried in the sun and returned to the same curd each evening for three days until the liquid is gone. Dry them in patchy weather and they mould rather than cure. The source list marks this vegan, which it is not; the cure is salted curd and the row carries the milk allergen accordingly.

name: Pesara Punugulu
description: The batter is ground thick enough to hold its shape on a spoon and no thinner, because punugulu slid into oil from a loose batter flatten into discs instead of puffing into balls. Oil at a moderate heat matters more here than in most frying: too hot and the outside sets brown while the moong inside stays raw and pasty, which is the failure you only find out about at the first bite. The onion is added to the batter at the last minute, since salted onion sitting in batter waters it down within twenty minutes. Moong carries this to 12.8 g of protein a serving, unusually high for a fried snack.

name: Hirekayi Palya
description: Ridge gourd holds so much water that it needs no added liquid at all, and the whole technique is getting rid of what it releases: cook it uncovered on a high flame for the first four minutes so the steam escapes, then lower and cover. Covered from the start it stews in its own juice and collapses into a grey slush. The coconut goes in at the very end off the heat, because cooked coconut in a palya turns gritty and loses the sweetness that balances the gourd. At 134 kcal a serving, most of it the tempering oil, and the hing is what keeps it off a gluten-free plate.

name: Half Fry Anda
description: The pan goes on medium and stays there; the white sets from the bottom up and high heat browns and toughens the underside before the top has gone from clear to opaque. Crack each egg into a cup first rather than onto the pan, which is the only reliable way to keep a broken yolk out of the other three. Salt goes on the white and not the yolk, since salt on a runny yolk leaves visible pale speckles where it sits. Two eggs a head with a tablespoon and a half of oil comes to 19.8 g of fat and 1.3 g of carbohydrate, which is about as cleanly keto as anything in the corpus.

name: Uzhunnu Vada
description: Urad dal is ground with as little water as the grinder will tolerate and then beaten by hand for several minutes, and that beating rather than the grinding is what puts air in; a spoonful of properly beaten batter floats in water and a spoonful of under-beaten batter sinks. Shape them on a wet palm, not a dry one, and make the hole before the vada leaves your hand, because the hole is what lets the middle cook through at the same rate as the edge. Batter that has sat an hour will not shape at all and is only good for punugulu. At 13.4 g of protein a serving the urad dal does more work here than the frying does, which is easy to forget about a deep-fried snack.
