name: Thoran
description: The coconut is crushed with the garlic, cumin and green chilli rather than simply grated in, and that pounding is what makes a thoran instead of a cabbage stir-fry with coconut on top; the oils come out of the coconut and coat everything. It is cooked covered on low with no water at all for eight minutes, then uncovered to dry, because cabbage that has boiled goes sulphurous and grey. Shallots rather than onion, and they are not browned. Fat is 65 per cent of calories on the coconut and the oil together, which clears the keto fat line, but carbohydrate at 13.7 g keeps the tag off the row.

name: Majjige
description: The Kannada majjige is the tempered one: mustard, curry leaf and a split green chilli are popped in a spoon of oil and poured over the thinned curd, which is what separates it from the plain Andhra and Tamil versions. The tempering has to be cooled for a minute before it goes in, because hot oil hitting cold buttermilk curdles it into visible flecks that no amount of whisking will redissolve. Thin it to the point where it pours like water rather than cream, roughly one part curd to four of water. At 35 kcal a tumbler it is a drink rather than a food, and the fat sits at 59 percent of calories, inside the band v2 leaves untagged.

name: Kuchalakki Ganji
description: Broken rice is used rather than whole grain because the fractured pieces release starch fast and thicken the water into something between a soup and a porridge, which whole rice will not do in forty minutes. The cooking water is never drained; that starchy liquid is the ganji and pouring it away leaves you with wet rice. Stir it in the last ten minutes or it catches and scorches on the base, and a scorched ganji tastes of nothing else. This is night food in Karnataka farming households, about 215 kcal a bowl, and it is deliberately thin enough to drink from the vessel.

name: Kerala Chaya
description: There are no spices in this at all, which is the whole difference from a masala chai; what it has instead is the pull, poured from one vessel to another from a height half a dozen times until it foams. That is not showmanship, it aerates the tea and cools it to drinking temperature in one action, and chaya served without it tastes flat and scalds. The leaves are boiled hard rather than steeped, which is why the dust grade is used and why the brew is strong enough to take a lot of milk. About 72 kcal a glass, almost all of it the milk and the four teaspoons of sugar.

name: Malabar Chicken Biryani
description: Malabar biryani uses short-grain jeerakasala rather than basmati and the rice is fried in ghee before it is boiled, which is what keeps the small grains separate instead of collapsing into each other under the dum. The rice is drained at seventy per cent cooked, still hard at the centre, because it finishes in the steam of the sealed pot and rice boiled through beforehand comes out as pilaf. Twenty minutes of dum on the lowest possible flame with a weight on the lid, and it is not opened once, since every peek costs the steam that is doing the cooking. Six servings at 37 g of protein each, the highest-protein row authored so far and the first layered rice dish in the corpus.

name: Ladies Finger Poriyal
description: The okra is fried in the oil for a full six minutes before anything wet or powdered joins it, which sets the cut faces and is the only reliable way to keep a poriyal from going ropey. Coconut is stirred in off the heat rather than cooked, so it stays sweet and white instead of browning into the dish. Chana dal in the tempering is the Tamil marker and it should be properly gold, not blond, since half-fried dal is chalky and you find every piece. Carbohydrate comes to 10.8 g and fat to 61 per cent of calories, so this misses keto by eight tenths of a gram, the third such near-miss in two batches.

name: Tindora nu Shaak
description: Every tindora is slit lengthways into quarters that stay joined at the stem, which lets the masala get inside without the pieces falling apart in the pan. Sort them before you cut: a tindora with red pulp at the centre is over-ripe, tastes soapy and will not soften, and one of those spoils a whole shaak. It cooks covered on low for twelve minutes with no water, because tindora is dense and dry and browning it hard before it is cooked through leaves a raw crunch in the middle. Carbohydrate lands at 8.0 g and fat at 67 per cent of calories, so this one clears the keto bar the source list claims for it, by a wider margin than anything in the last two batches.

Made properly the pulikachal keeps a fortnight, so the paste is worth making at three times this quantity.

name: Poori
description: The dough is kneaded stiff, noticeably tighter than a chapati dough, because a soft dough drinks oil and comes out heavy instead of puffing. Roll each poori to an even thickness with no thin patches; a thin spot lets steam escape and that poori will lie flat in the oil while its neighbours balloon. Press it under the oil with the back of a slotted spoon for the first two seconds, which is what forces the puff. Roughly 60 ml of oil is actually absorbed across twelve pooris, not the two cups they swim in, which still brings each serving to 14.7 g of fat.

name: Malabar Parotta
description: The whole dish is one long gluten development and then one act of lamination: the dough is kneaded wet and slapped for ten minutes, rested two hours under oil, then each ball is stretched translucent on an oiled counter, pleated into a rope and coiled. Rush the rest and the dough tears when you stretch it, which loses every layer. Cook on a medium tawa, not hot, since high heat sets the outside before the inner layers have steamed apart. The crush at the end is not optional showmanship; clapping the hot parotta between your palms is what separates the layers you spent two hours building.

description: This is a rasam built on chicken stock rather than dal water, so the bones are simmered first and the tamarind added to the strained liquid rather than cooked with the meat, which would make the broth cloudy and slightly bitter. description: The masala is roasted dry and then ground with fresh coconut and a little tamarind, and roasting the coconut separately from the spices matters, because coconut browns in about ninety seconds and burnt coconut turns the whole sukka bitter with no way back. Sukka means dry, so the pan is finished uncovered until the masala clings to the chicken rather than pooling under it. Byadgi chillies give the deep red without the heat, and the heat here comes from pepper instead. At 11.1 g of carbohydrate and 57 per cent of calories from fat it misses the keto tag on both tests rather than the usual one, and the source list marks it true.

Only after that does the shoot behave like a vegetable. It stays faintly sour on its own, which is why the jaggery and tamarind both go in. Available for about six weeks after the first monsoon rains and essentially unobtainable fresh otherwise.

name: Chai
description: Plain chai lives or dies on when the milk goes in. Boil the water with the tea leaves and ginger first and give it a full two minutes, because leaves dropped into milk never release properly and the cup comes out pale and flat. Once the milk is in, bring it up and pull it back three times rather than letting it boil steadily, which is what builds the colour without making the tea bitter. Sugar goes in with the milk, not at the end, so it dissolves into the body rather than sitting at the bottom of the glass. About 69 kcal a cup, nearly all of it the milk and sugar, and it is not suitable for anyone lactose intolerant.

name: Bharwa Karela
description: The gourds are scraped, slit, salted and left half an hour, and the dark water they give up takes a good part of the bitterness with it; squeeze them hard and the difference is the whole dish. The stuffing is cooked before it goes in, because raw besan and amchur inside a closed gourd never lose their rawness however long the pan runs. Tie each one with thread rather than trusting it to hold, and turn them only every four minutes so one face browns properly at a time. At 16.7 g of carbohydrate the row misses LOW_CARB as well as the keto flag the source claims, though the fat proportion clears easily; the besan and the two onions are where that carbohydrate is.

description: Soaked rice and a fixed one-to-one-and-a-half water ratio, cooked covered and then left sealed off the heat, because a pulao stirred while it steams turns to khichdi. The vegetables go in raw with the rice rather than being sautéed first, which is what keeps the carrot and beans distinct instead of collapsing into the grain. A teaspoon of sugar and a squeeze of lemon at the end are the Gujarati signature and they are what separate this from a North Indian pulao made with the same vegetables. Roughly 430 kcal a serving, and it is the rice rather than the five vegetables carrying almost all of it.

name: Naan
description: Curd and a pinch of soda do the work a tandoor's yeast culture would, and the two hours of rest is where the sourness and the stretch both come from; an hour gives you a slightly chewy flatbread instead. The tawa must be genuinely hot and dry, and the trick is to wet one face of the rolled naan with water and lay that face down, so it sticks to the pan and lets you invert the whole tawa over the flame to blister the top the way a tandoor wall would. Rolled thin it will not bubble; a naan wants to be thicker than you think. Contains curd and butter, so despite the source list marking this vegan it is not.

name: Bili Motte
description: Start the eggs in cold water rather than dropping them into boiling, because the thermal shock cracks the shell and a plume of white escapes into the pan. Eight minutes from the moment it reaches a boil gives a yolk that is set through but still bright yellow; at eleven it goes chalky with a grey ring. The ice bath afterwards is not optional, since it both stops the cooking and contracts the white away from the membrane, which is the whole difference between a shell that peels in two pieces and one that takes the egg with it. At 156 kcal for two eggs with 13 g of protein and 63 percent of calories from fat, it clears the house keto threshold.

name: Karela Bharwa
description: Salting the scraped gourds and leaving them forty minutes is the step people skip and then complain about bitterness; the salt draws out a visible brown liquid that carries most of the momordicin with it. Squeeze them out properly afterwards, because any water left inside turns the besan stuffing to sludge the moment it goes in. Tie each stuffed gourd with thread rather than trusting it to hold, and cook them covered on the lowest flame turning every four minutes, since bitter gourd skin scorches long before the inside is done. name: Rava Upma
description: Rava is dry-roasted first until it smells nutty and the grains move freely, and that step alone is the difference between upma and paste; unroasted semolina absorbs water in clumps that never come apart. The water goes in at a rolling boil and the rava is rained in with one hand while the other stirs continuously, never the reverse. Two and a half parts water to one of rava for a soft upma, two parts for a firm one, and there is no correcting it later. It sets as it cools, so it is served straight from the pan rather than held.

description: Akuri is pulled off the heat while it still looks underdone, glossy and barely holding together, because the residual heat in the pan finishes it in the thirty seconds it takes to reach the table; cooked until it looks right in the pan it arrives dry. The heat stays low throughout and the eggs are stirred constantly with a flat spoon, scraping rather than folding. A spoonful of milk beaten into the eggs buys a little more margin before they tighten. This is the wet, creamy end of the scrambled egg family, which is what separates it from a bhurji cooked dry.

description: Each pod is slit down one side and left whole, and the besan masala is packed in dry rather than made into a paste, because a wet stuffing steams inside the pod and the whole thing goes slimy from the inside out. The pods are laid in one layer and turned only every five minutes; crowded or stirred, they break open and the stuffing ends up in the pan instead of the okra. Sesame and coconut in the masala are the Gujarati markers and neither belongs in a Punjabi bharwa bhindi.

name: Bafela Eeda
description: The Gujarati version is served warm rather than cold and dressed while still hot, which is why the eggs come out of the water at seven minutes with a yolk that is just set at the edge and slightly fudgy at the centre. Add a teaspoon of salt to the boiling water; it does not season the egg through the shell but it does coagulate any white that escapes a hairline crack and stops it streaming out. Dress them the moment they are peeled, because chaat masala and lemon slide straight off a cold egg but cling to a warm one. Two eggs come to 164 kcal with 13 g of protein and 62 percent of calories from fat.

name: Tovve
description: Tovve is defined by what is left out: no onion, no garlic, no tomato, no sambar powder, just toor dal cooked soft with turmeric and green chilli and finished with coconut and a vaghar. That restraint is the point and adding a masala to it makes a different dish. Mash the dal properly against the side of the pot rather than whisking it, since whisked dal goes gluey and thin at the same time. The jaggery and lemon go in off the heat together and are what stop it tasting flat. This is the everyday Karnataka dal eaten with hot rice and a spoon of ghee.

Break the cold rice up with wet fingers before it goes near the pan; lumps put into hot oil stay lumps. The peanuts are fried first and lifted out, since left in they soften in the steam from the rice and lose the only crunch the dish has. Sugar and lemon at the end, as in every Gujarati row here, and a bhat without them tastes like plain fried rice.

name: Urulaikizhangu Roast
description: Boil the potatoes whole in their skins and cool them completely before peeling and cubing, because warm potato crumbles the moment it meets a spatula and you end up roasting mash. A tablespoon of rice flour tossed through the cubes is what gives the crust; without it the surface browns but never crisps. The pan stays wide, uncovered and barely stirred, once every five minutes at most, since every stir knocks off the crust that has just formed. Sesame oil rather than any other, which is the Tamil marker and is not interchangeable here.

description: The tomato bed is cooked down until it is thick enough to hold a hollow pressed into it with a spoon, and that test is the whole timing of the dish; a loose base lets the eggs sink and disperse instead of sitting. Take it off while the yolks still move under the skin. A teaspoon of sugar in the tomatoes is the Gujarati touch and it is doing acidity work rather than sweetening.

name: Eeda nu Shaak

name: Puzhungiya Mutta
description: In Kerala these are boiled hard, to nine minutes rather than seven or eight, because they are usually going into a curry or a puttu plate afterwards and a soft yolk disintegrates in gravy. Crack the shell all over before peeling instead of picking at one end, which lets water seep under the membrane and lifts the whole shell in a sheet. A pinch of turmeric in the boiling water is the local habit; it stains the shell rather than the egg and simply makes cracked ones easy to spot. At 156 kcal for two eggs, 63 percent of calories from fat and 1.4 g of carbohydrate, it is a straightforwardly keto row.

name: Bataka Poha
description: The potato must be diced small and fried to a set crust before the poha goes anywhere near the pan, because a potato added at the same time as the flakes is either raw or has been stirred long enough to break them. Gujarati poha carries a definite sweetness from sugar and a sourness from lemon, and both go in at the end, off the heat, or the sugar catches on the base. Rinse the thick poha rather than soaking it and fold it in with a spatula from underneath rather than stirring. At 348 kcal a serving with 46 g of carbohydrate it is a high-carb breakfast, which the source row correctly flags.

name: Vankaya Vepudu
description: Brinjal cut and left standing browns and goes bitter, so it is cubed straight into the hot oil and not before; a bowl of cut brinjal waiting on the counter is the commonest reason this dish tastes off. It takes more oil than looks reasonable because brinjal is a sponge, and holding back on the oil gives dry leathery cubes rather than silky ones. The pan is left uncovered throughout so the pieces fry rather than steam. Salt goes in late, after the cubes have collapsed, since salted early it draws water and the vepudu boils.

name: Thengapal Kanji
description: Thick coconut milk goes in at the very end with the pot already off the heat, because boiled coconut milk splits into oil and curd and no amount of stirring brings it back together. The rice is cooked in water first and taken further than you would for plain rice, until the grains have burst and thickened their own liquid. Shallots rather than onion, barely softened, and the whole thing stays deliberately pale and sweet-ish. This is convalescent food in Kerala and it is meant to be thin enough to drink.

name: Potato Roast
description: Parboil the potatoes whole in their skins and cool them completely before cutting, because a hot cube crumbles at the edges and those crumbs are what stick to the pan and burn. The rice flour dusted on just before frying is what gives the shell its crackle; without it the cubes go soft in their own steam within five minutes of leaving the heat. Spread them in one layer and leave them alone for three full minutes at a time, since every stir resets the crust. At 277 kcal a serving with 52 percent of calories from sesame oil, it is medium-carb rather than low, and the asafoetida keeps it off a gluten-free plate.

name: Podi Idli
description: Day-old idlis work better than fresh ones, which is the whole reason the dish exists; a fresh idli is too wet and tears when it is tossed, while one that has firmed up overnight holds its cube. The podi is stirred into hot oil off the heat rather than sprinkled dry, so it coats instead of dusting and falling off. Every dal in the podi is roasted separately because chana and urad brown at different rates and one pan means one of them is either pale or burnt. Toss the cubes in the pan for barely a minute; longer and the podi catches and turns acrid.

description: The coconut is roasted on its own and taken only to light brown, since it crosses from gold to burnt in about ninety seconds and burnt coconut makes the whole sukka bitter with no way back. Boiled eggs are halved rather than left whole and laid cut side down in the masala for the last two minutes, which is the only way the yolk tastes of anything. name: Poha Chevdo
description: Thin poha and only thin poha; the thick variety used for upma absorbs oil and stays chewy instead of puffing. The oil must be properly hot and the poha goes in for about eight seconds in a wire basket, long enough to swell and turn white and no longer, because at fifteen seconds it browns and tastes burnt. Everything else is fried separately and at its own temperature, then tossed together only when all of it is cold. Salt and sugar are sprinkled over the cold mixture, since added warm they draw moisture and the chevdo goes soft inside a day.

name: Uduku Guddu
description: Andhra households boil these to eight minutes and then slit rather than halve them, so a paste of chilli powder, salt and a little oil can be worked into the cut and the egg still holds together on the plate. The slit has to go into a fully cooled egg; cut warm, the yolk smears along the blade and the karam paste sits on the outside instead of inside. A splash of vinegar in the boiling water helps any leaked white set fast rather than clouding the pan. Two eggs with the karam come to 183 kcal at 67 percent of calories from fat, which clears the house keto threshold.

name: Boiled Egg
description: Everything about a boiled egg is timing and the cool-down. Eight minutes from the boil is the general-purpose setting: yolk firm, no grey ring, still moist enough to mash. The ice bath matters more than the water temperature you started at, because it is contraction rather than cooking that separates the white from the shell membrane, and a peeled-warm egg will always tear. Older eggs peel more easily than fresh ones, so if a batch fights you it is the eggs and not the method. Two eggs give 156 kcal, 13 g of protein and 63 percent of calories from fat, with 1.3 g of carbohydrate.

name: Ulli Karam Guddu
description: This is the ulli karam paste cooked out rather than used raw, and the cooking is what changes it; twelve minutes in oil takes the onion from sharp to sweet and the whole thing stops tasting like a condiment. Slash the boiled eggs before they go in, or the karam sits on the outside and the yolk tastes of nothing. Keep the pan dry, adding no water at all, so the paste clings to the eggs rather than becoming a gravy. Sesame oil is not interchangeable here; it is doing as much of the flavour as the chillies are.

name: Dhansak
description: Three dals and two vegetables are cooked to complete collapse and then passed through a mouli or beaten smooth, because a dhansak with recognisable pieces of pumpkin in it has been stopped too early; the vegetables are there to disappear into the texture. The mutton is browned separately and returned at the end rather than cooked in the dal, which would leave it stringy and the dal grey. Tamarind and jaggery go in together at the finish and the balance between them is the dish; too little tamarind and it tastes like a heavy dal. Seventy minutes of cooking and the only row in the corpus at premium cost tier besides row 101.

name: Oats Dosa
description: This is an instant batter with no fermentation, so it has to be thin, thinner than a regular dosa batter and closer to buttermilk, and it is poured onto the tawa from a ladle held high rather than spread with the back of it. Stir the batter before every single dosa, because the oats and rava sink within about a minute and the last dosa comes out thick and the first one watery.

name: Dalitoy
description: The GSB dalitoy is deliberately bare: toor dal, green chilli, asafoetida and a coconut oil tempering, with no onion, no garlic and no tomato, and the restraint is the point rather than an omission. Cook the dal past the point where it holds shape and then whisk it rather than mashing, which gives a pourable consistency without turning it gluey. The tempering goes over at the table, so the mustard and curry leaf are still crackling when the dal reaches the plate. At 206 kcal a serving with 8.8 g of protein it is a plain, filling dal, and the asafoetida is the only thing keeping it off a gluten-free plate.

description: The Andhra burji runs hotter and drier than the Karnataka one: the onion is browned properly rather than just softened, and the egg goes in with the pan hot enough that it sets in curds instead of turning creamy. Beat the eggs only until the yolk breaks and no further, because an over-beaten egg holds air, sets rubbery and then weeps water into the pan. Pull it off while it still looks slightly underdone; residual pan heat takes it the rest of the way in the thirty seconds it takes to reach the table. At 336 kcal a serving with 15 g of protein and 71 percent of calories from fat, the fat clears the house keto floor but the onion and tomato put carbohydrate just over the line.

name: Masala Khichu
description: Rice flour goes into water that is already at a hard rolling boil and is beaten in with one hand while the other keeps stirring, because water that has come off the boil produces lumps that no amount of later work removes. It is beaten against the side of the pot rather than stirred, for a full four minutes, until it comes away in one glossy mass. Then it is covered and left on the lowest flame so the residual steam cooks the flour through; this is where a khichu goes from tasting of raw flour to tasting of nothing else. Served in the bowl with oil poured over and chilli powder on top, and it sets hard within twenty minutes.

name: Namkeen Lassi
description: Salted lassi is thicker than buttermilk and thinner than sweet lassi, roughly two parts curd to one of water, and it is churned rather than whisked so that it comes up with a real head of foam. Use a mathani or a blender on its lowest setting; a high-speed blender warms the curd, and warm curd separates into grain and whey within minutes of standing. Roasted cumin goes in ground rather than whole and after churning, since whole seeds trap in the foam and sit on the lip of the glass. At 76 kcal a glass with 4.4 g of protein, it is heavier than chaas and sits at 49 percent of calories from fat, short of the house keto threshold.

Grind the masala with the coconut and as little water as the mixie will take. Lemon at the very end, off the heat.

name: Yetti Tawa Fry
description: Prawns cook in about ninety seconds a side and everything else about this recipe is arranged around that; the masala is a thick paste rather than a marinade precisely because there is no time for anything to penetrate. Dry the prawns on a cloth before the paste goes on or it slides off in the pan. Rice flour is what gives the crust, and the tawa must be hot before they go anywhere near it. Overcooked prawns go from tender to rubbery inside thirty seconds and there is no recovering them, so pull them the moment they curl into a C rather than a tight O.

description: Bhuna means the frying, and the whole method is to keep the pan dry and let the chicken cook in its own released liquid until that liquid has gone; no water is added at any point. The lid stays off from start to finish, which is what people get wrong, because covering it produces a perfectly good curry and not this. Three onions look like too many until they have cooked down to almost nothing and become the coating. The last ten minutes are on high with constant turning, and that is where the colour comes from.

name: Pongali
description: The moong dal is dry-roasted before it goes anywhere near water, and skipping that is the difference between pongali and a savoury khichdi; roasted dal smells nutty and holds its shape while unroasted dal dissolves. It is cooked deliberately wet, about five parts water to one of grain, because pongali stiffens as it sits and one served at the right consistency in the pot is a brick at the table. Peppercorns go in whole and are meant to be bitten. Most of the ghee goes in at the end rather than the start.

name: Meen Varuval
description: The marinade has to sit on dry fish, so the fillets are patted with a cloth and salted for ten minutes and then patted again before the masala goes near them, because a wet surface turns the paste into a sauce that slides off in the pan. name: Muddha Pappu
description: This is toor dal cooked to collapse and mashed to a paste with nothing in it at all except turmeric and salt, which is exactly why the dal has to be washed properly and cooked with enough water; there is no masala to hide behind. Mash it against the side of the vessel with a wooden masher while it is hot, because cooled dal resists and comes out lumpy. name: Guddu Vepudu
description: The eggs are boiled, halved and then fried cut side down in the masala until the yolk face takes a crust, which is the whole dish; left whole they roll around and come out coated in nothing. The masala stays dry throughout and no water goes in at any point. Fry the chilli powder in oil for a few seconds before the eggs go in rather than dusting it over them, since raw chilli powder on a boiled egg tastes exactly like raw chilli powder. Onion is optional here and many households leave it out entirely.

name: Egg Podimas
description: Podimas means crumbled, and the whole point is a dry, fine crumb rather than the soft curds of a burji, so the eggs are hard-boiled first and grated on the coarse side of a box grater rather than scrambled in the pan. Grated warm they compact into a paste, so they have to be fully cold before they meet the grater. The crumb then goes into the tempering for barely two minutes, long enough to take on the turmeric and the curry leaf and no longer, because reheated egg protein tightens and squeaks. At 217 kcal a serving with 11 g of protein and 71 percent of calories from fat, it clears the house keto threshold.

name: Gawar nu Shaak
description: Cluster beans are bitter and fibrous, and both are dealt with in the prep rather than the pan: snap the ends and pull the string down both edges, and choose young pods that break cleanly instead of bending. A pod that bends is old and no amount of cooking softens it. They need longer covered than most Gujarati shaaks, about fifteen minutes, because the pods are dense. Jaggery is not present here and the sugar is doing the work of placing the bitterness rather than covering it.

name: Karela nu Shaak
description: Sliced thin and salted for half an hour, then squeezed hard; the dark water that comes out is most of the bitterness and squeezing properly is the entire technique. Do not rinse afterwards, which washes the seasoning out along with nothing else. The slices are then fried in a wide pan until the edges have crisped, because a soft karela tastes considerably more bitter than a browned one. Jaggery and amchur go in together at the end, and the shaak is meant to end up sweet, sour and bitter at once rather than with the bitterness hidden.

name: Onion Paratha
description: Salt the chopped onion and leave it twenty minutes, then squeeze it dry, and that squeeze is the whole recipe; onion salted into the filling at the last minute weeps inside the paratha and tears it open on the tawa every time. Chop it fine enough that no piece is thicker than the dough will tolerate. Roll gently from the centre outwards rather than pressing, and if a small tear opens patch it with a pinch of dry flour rather than starting again. description: Soak the granules in hot water, then squeeze them out twice and discard both lots of water, because the first soak carries off the beany smell that otherwise runs through the whole dish. Squeeze them properly dry as well, since waterlogged granules dilute the masala and refuse to brown. name: Bread Pakora
description: Day-old bread, always; fresh bread collapses in the batter and comes out of the oil as an oily flap. The batter has to be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon and stay there, because a thin batter slides off the crumb and fries in the oil on its own. name: Poro
description: The Parsi-Gujarati poro is thicker than a French omelette and cooked through rather than folded, so it goes into a pan that is hot but not fierce and then straight down to low, because the outside sets long before a 2 cm thick egg cake is done at the centre. Beat the eggs with a fork rather than a whisk; a whisk incorporates air, the poro rises in the pan and then collapses into a rubbery disc as it cools. The onion must be chopped very fine and added raw, since diced onion releases water as it cooks and the poro tears when it is turned. At 324 kcal a serving with 14 g of protein and 73 percent of calories from fat, it clears the house keto threshold.

name: Papeta Par Eeda
description: The potatoes are cut into matchsticks and fried until they are properly cooked and browned before the eggs go anywhere near them, because there is no rescuing undercooked potato once four eggs are sitting on top of it. Press the fried straws down into an even bed and make wells with the back of a spoon so the eggs sit rather than run through. name: Kalakki
description: Kalakki is a half-boiled egg broken into a hot pan and stirred exactly twice, so the white sets in ribbons while the yolk stays liquid and runs when it is cut. Two stirs is literal: a third turns it into a scramble and the dish loses its name. The pan wants black pepper hitting hot oil for a few seconds before the egg goes in, since pepper added afterwards sits on the surface and tastes raw. It is eaten straight out of the pan with parotta, and at 311 kcal for two eggs with 76 percent of calories from fat, it is one of the cleanest keto rows in the corpus.

name: Bataka nu Shaak
description: Raw potato goes straight into the vaghar rather than being boiled first, which is what separates a Gujarati bataka nu shaak from every other potato dish; boiled potato added to a tempering only ever tastes of two things that met late. Cut the cubes small and keep the pan covered on low so they cook through in their own steam. There is no onion and no garlic in this at all. Sugar and lemon at the end, and it should read sweet before it reads spicy, which is the point people miss when they scale the chilli up.

name: Alasandala Vepudu
description: Cowpeas are boiled to the point where they give under a thumb but still hold their skins, and that window is narrow; a minute past it and the vepudu is a mash. Drain them properly and let the steam come off before they go into the pan, because wet peas will not fry and simply reheat. The popu goes in first and the peas join a pan that is already fragrant, not the other way round. Coconut goes in off the heat. Overnight soaking is not optional; an unsoaked cowpea takes twice as long and cooks unevenly.

name: Mutta Mappas
description: Mappas means a coconut milk gravy and the entire discipline of the dish is that it must never boil once the milk is in; a bare shiver at the edge of the pan is as far as it goes, and a rolling boil splits it into oil and curd within seconds. Thin coconut milk goes in first and can simmer, thick milk goes in last and off the heat. Whole black pepper rather than chilli carries most of the heat, which is what makes this taste Syrian Christian rather than generic. Eggs go in halved at the very end.

name: Jalebi
description: Two temperatures and both matter: the oil at a moderate 165 so the coils cook through without darkening, and the syrup warm rather than hot, because a hot syrup makes the jalebi go soft and a cold one will not soak in at all. The soak is fifteen seconds, no more, and that is the whole difference between a crisp jalebi and a wet one. Syrup must be one-thread consistency; test it between finger and thumb rather than trusting a clock. Batter fermented overnight gives the sourness the sugar is there to balance.

name: Pattani Sundal
description: The peas must hold their shape, so they are boiled until just tender and checked from fifteen minutes; a sundal made with split, mushy peas is a different and worse dish, and there is no way back once they have gone. Drain them fully and let them steam dry before they go into the tempering. Coconut is stirred in off the heat and stays white. This is temple food and prasadam food, made in quantity during Navaratri, and it is eaten warm from a paper cone rather than as a side.

description: Semolina drinks water for a good twenty minutes after mixing, so the batter is rested and then loosened again immediately before cooking; skip the second thinning and the last chilla is a thick pancake. It is spread with the back of a ladle rather than poured, which is what distinguishes a chilla from a dosa, and it is meant to be thick enough to hold the chopped vegetables in place. Cook it slowly, four minutes on the first side, because a chilla browned fast has raw besan in the middle.

name: Millet Dosa
description: Ragi has no gluten and very little starch structure, so the rice and urad are doing all the binding and the proportions are not adjustable downwards; a batter with more millet than this tears on the tawa and will not lift. Ferment it as you would a plain dosa batter, but expect less rise, since millet ferments more slowly and a batter that has only risen a third is still ready. The tawa needs to be hotter than for a rice dosa because the batter is heavier. It browns fast and darkly, which is the millet and not a mistake.

name: Shami Kebab
description: The mixture has to be cooked completely dry before it is ground, and that is the step every failed shami kebab skipped; a trace of moisture left in the pan means kebabs that fall apart in the oil however much egg goes in afterwards. Grind it while it is still warm and it comes together smooth. Chill the shaped patties a full hour before frying, since a cold kebab holds and a room-temperature one spreads. Chana dal is structural rather than a filler, and the ratio of about one part dal to five of meat is what makes it bind at all.

name: Kozhi Kuzhambu
description: Fennel is the marker and it goes in twice, whole into the oil and ground into the coconut masala, and a kozhi kuzhambu without it tastes like a curry from somewhere else. The coconut and spices are roasted separately and ground with water into a fine paste rather than a coarse one, because a gritty masala never smooths out into the gravy. Sesame oil rather than any other. Shallots, not onion, and a dozen of them, which is what gives the gravy its body without any thickener at all.

Crush the mustard seeds rather than powdering them; ground fine they turn acrid. The fish goes in for the last eight minutes only and is not stirred at all, just spooned over, because kingfish steaks break up the moment anything moves them. Mustard oil must be smoked and cooled first or the whole pan tastes raw.

name: Moru Curry
description: Curd curdles the moment it boils and there is no recovering it, so the pan comes off the heat before the curd goes in and goes back only to the barest warmth. Whisk the curd with the ground coconut paste first rather than adding them separately, which gives the mixture something to hold on to. description: Marrow bones rather than meat, or at least mostly bones, because the point of the soup is what comes out of them and a lean cut gives you thin, grey water. name: Langar Wali Dal
description: Whole black urad with the skins on, not the split white dal, and the skins are what give the colour and most of the body. Ninety minutes at a bare simmer after pressure cooking is not padding; the dal only turns creamy in the last half hour and stopping at tender leaves you with something that tastes thin. Mash a ladleful against the side every fifteen minutes rather than blending, which turns it grey and gluey. There is no cream in this and there never was, whatever restaurant versions do; the texture comes from time.

name: Miriyala Charu
description: This is the pepper rasam given to people who are unwell, so the pepper is coarsely pounded rather than powdered and it goes in at the end: boiled for more than a minute it turns acrid instead of warming. The tamarind water must come to a boil and cook out its raw edge for a good six minutes before the dal water joins it, and the whole thing must never boil again after that, only froth at the edges. A rolling boil is what makes a charu cloudy and flat. At 78 kcal a serving it is barely food, which is the point, and the asafoetida keeps it off a gluten-free plate.

name: Mini Idli
description: Mini idlis steam in six minutes rather than twelve, and the usual mistake is giving them the full time out of habit, which dries them to pellets. The batter needs to be a shade thinner than for full idlis so it levels in the small moulds; too thick and each one steams with a peak and a dense centre. Grease the plates properly, because a mini idli has far more surface area for its volume and sticks far more readily. At 228 kcal a serving with 48 g of carbohydrate it is a high-carb tiffin, and being steamed and fermented it is one of the easiest rows in the corpus to digest.

description: The gojju is made first and thick, and the poha goes in dry rather than being washed or soaked, which is the opposite of every other poha dish; the tamarind mixture carries enough moisture to soften it and washing it first gives you a paste. Leave it twenty minutes off the heat afterwards and it comes to the right texture on its own. The powdered masala of roasted coriander, sesame and chilli is ground fresh and is what makes this taste of Mysore rather than of tamarind rice.

description: Chana dal and bottle gourd cook at completely different rates, so the dal is soaked for two hours and pressure-cooked to nearly done before the gourd goes in at all; added together, the gourd disintegrates while the dal is still chalky. Dudhi releases a great deal of water, which means the dal should be left slightly thicker than you want it, because it thins itself in the last five minutes. The Gujarati balance wants a little jaggery against the lemon, added at the end so neither cooks out. At 283 kcal a serving with 9 g of protein it is a substantial side, and the asafoetida keeps it off a gluten-free plate.

name: Motte Gassi
description: A gassi is built on a wet-ground coconut masala, which means the coconut and the roasted chillies must be ground with as little water as possible and then thinned in the pan, not ground thin to begin with; a watery grind never emulsifies and the gravy splits into oil and liquid. Boiled eggs are slit and slipped in only for the last three minutes, because an egg simmered in gravy goes rubbery and the yolk chalks. Byadgi chillies give the colour without the heat, which is why the count looks alarmingly high. name: Kerala Dosa
description: Thinner and softer than the crisp Udupi kind, and the batter is ground looser to match, pourable rather than spreadable. Rice and urad dal are ground separately because the dal needs twenty minutes of whipping to a foam while the rice only needs breaking to a grit. The tawa must be seasoned and then cooled slightly with a wipe of water before every dosa, since batter poured onto a pan at full heat seizes before it can spread. About 10.6 g of protein a serving from the dal, and the ferment is what makes it the most digestible thing on a South Indian breakfast table.

name: Meen Rava Fry
description: Rava rather than rice flour, which is the Karnataka coastal signature and the reason this one is not gluten free where most Indian fish fries are. Press the semolina on firmly and then let the coated fish stand five minutes so it hydrates and sticks, since rava dusted on and fried immediately falls off into the oil. Mackerel is oily enough to need no more than a medium pan, and a hot one scorches the crust before the flesh is through. Around 26 g of protein a serving, and the crust should be sandy and audible rather than smooth.

name: Kathol
description: A mixed-pulse curry rather than a dal, and the mix is the difficulty: chana takes twice as long as moong, so either they soak overnight together and get pressure-cooked to the slowest one, or the quick ones turn to mush waiting. Sprouting them for a day instead of soaking is the Gujarati preference and makes them noticeably easier on the stomach. Jaggery and lemon go in at the end together, and the balance between them is what stops it tasting like plain boiled beans. About 11 g of protein and nearly 8 g of fibre a serving, which is the most fibre in the corpus.

name: Chana Dal Lauki
description: The North Indian version leans on a bhuna base rather than a tempering: onion, ginger and tomato are cooked down until the oil separates before anything else joins them, and that reduction is what gives the dish its body without cream or coconut. Chana dal is soaked and cooked apart from the lauki for the same reason it always is, because the gourd turns to water in the time the dal needs. Finish with garam masala off the heat rather than frying it, which cooks the volatile spices straight out. At 282 kcal a serving with 9 g of protein, it is a substantial side, and the hing is what keeps it off a gluten-free plate.

Shallots rather than onion, and a great deal of them, since they sweeten as they cook where onion would only soften. About 388 kcal a serving, finished with a spoon of sesame oil over the top, which is not optional to how it tastes.

name: Ganthiya Sambharo Nasto
description: A plate rather than a dish: bought ganthiya alongside a warm shredded cabbage and carrot sambharo, which is Gujarat's standard morning nasto. The sambharo is stir-fried for barely four minutes and must stay crunchy, because a soft sambharo beside a crisp ganthiya is the whole thing undone. Mustard seeds have to pop properly before the cabbage goes in, since they will not pop once the pan is full of wet vegetable. Assemble only at the table, as ganthiya sitting against warm cabbage goes limp within a few minutes.

name: Kambu Dosai
description: Pearl millet ferments faster and more violently than rice, so eight hours is usually enough and twelve will take it past sour into bitter, which is the opposite of the problem a rice dosa has. The batter is darker and heavier and will not spread as thin, so pour a smaller ladleful and accept a thicker dosa rather than fighting it. Kambu has no gluten and very little starch to bind, which is why the urad dal proportion is higher here than in a rice dosa. Around 14 g of protein and 12.5 g of fibre a serving, the highest fibre of any tiffin row.

name: Osaman
description: The thin broth poured off a pot of cooked toor dal, seasoned and served in its own right, which is why a Surti kitchen gets two dishes from one pot of dal. It must stay watery: thickened it becomes an ordinary dal and the point of it is lost. Jaggery and lemon go in together at the end in almost equal measure, and the sweetness should be noticeable rather than hidden. Around 112 kcal a serving, drunk from a bowl or poured over plain rice, and it is one of the few gravies here with no onion or garlic at all.

name: Kootanchoru
description: Nagercoil's one-pot of rice, two dals and whatever vegetables are in the house, and the trick is staging: the dals and hard vegetables go in first, the rice after, and the ground coconut paste only in the last ten minutes so it does not split. Everything is deliberately overcooked into one soft mass, which is the dish rather than a failure of it. The coconut paste is ground with pepper and cumin rather than chilli, so the heat sits at the back of the throat. About 310 kcal a serving, and it was built to use up the vegetable basket at the end of the week.

name: Chana nu Shaak
description: Kala chana rather than kabuli, which holds its shape through a long cook where the white chickpea goes floury, and it needs a full overnight soak with no shortcut that works. Pressure-cook it in the soaking water rather than fresh, since a good deal of the colour and flavour has already leached into it. The gravy is deliberately thin and the chana is left whole, so this eats as a shaak with rotli rather than as a thick chole. About 10 g of protein and 8 g of fibre a serving, with jaggery and lemon rounding it off in the Gujarati way.

name: Rumali Roti
description: Stretched rather than rolled past a point, and thrown between the hands the way pizza dough is, until it is thin enough to read through. The dough has to be softer and wetter than any other roti dough and then rested a full hour, because gluten that has not relaxed springs back and tears the moment it goes thin. It cooks on the outside of an inverted kadai in under a minute a side and is folded like a handkerchief while still warm, which is where the name comes from. About 282 kcal a serving, and the maida is why it is not gluten free.

name: Murgh Masala
description: Murgh masala is the plain house chicken curry, and the only technique in it is the bhuna: three onions cooked down slowly for a full fifteen minutes until they are deep brown and jammy, then the tomato reduced until the oil comes back out. Rushed, the onion is merely soft and the gravy stays thin and raw-tasting no matter how long it simmers afterwards. The chicken goes in unbrowned and cooks in the masala, which is why bone-in pieces matter; boneless breast in this dish dries out inside ten minutes. At 409 kcal a serving with 39 g of protein, the three onions and two tomatoes put carbohydrate at 16.7 g, over both the keto and the low-carb lines.

name: Fish Curry Punjabi
description: Yoghurt rather than coconut or tamarind, which is what separates the Punjabi curry from every coastal one, and it has to be whisked smooth and added off the heat or it splits into curds the moment it hits a hot pan. Ajwain is not optional here; it is the spice that makes fish taste Punjabi and it also settles the heaviness. The fish goes in only for the last eight minutes, since rohu breaks up if it is stirred through a gravy for any longer. About 27 g of protein a serving, and the gravy should coat the pieces rather than drown them.

name: Nati Koli Saaru
description: Country chicken is a different bird: tougher, darker and it wants forty minutes where broiler wants fifteen, and cooking it the short way gives stringy meat in a thin sauce. The masala is ground fresh with coconut and poppy seeds, and the poppy seeds are what thicken it rather than any flour. description: Parsi sweet, sour and hot all at once, and the three have to be balanced against each other rather than layered, so jaggery and vinegar go in together and get tasted as a pair. Prawns take four minutes and not a second more; past that they tighten into rubber and no amount of simmering softens them again. Make the gravy completely first, get it to the consistency you want, and only then put the prawns in. Around 31 g of protein a serving, and this is the first crustacean row in the corpus, which brings an allergen nothing else here carries.

description: No ground garam masala at all, which is what makes it taste unlike any other biryani: the heat and aroma come from raw green chilli, coriander and mint in quantity, and from onions fried almost to black. The rice is boiled separately to seventy per cent and then layered, so it finishes in the steam rather than in the gravy. Yoghurt goes into the marinade cold and the chicken sits in it an hour, which is what keeps it from drying out through the dum. About 21 g of protein a serving, and the green in it should be visible in the finished pot.

name: Sambaram Curry
description: A curd curry splits if it is allowed anywhere near a boil, so the heat goes down before the curd goes in and the pot never rises above a tremble afterwards. Whisking a spoon of rice flour into the curd first is the insurance most Kerala kitchens use; the starch holds the protein together even if the flame is misjudged. Coconut and cumin are ground and added before the curd rather than after, because the paste needs two minutes of cooking that the curd cannot survive. At 207 kcal a serving the coconut and oil supply 70 percent of the calories, but carbohydrate at 12 g keeps it off the keto list, and the source row marks it non-vegan correctly.
